I also report on online scams and offer advice to families and individuals about staying safe on the internet. Before joining PCMag, I wrote about tech and video games for CNN, Fanbyte, Mashable, The New York Times, and TechRadar. I also worked at CNN International, where I did field producing and reporting on sports that are popular with worldwide audiences. In addition to the categories below, I exclusively cover ad blockers, authenticator apps, hardware security keys, and private messaging apps.

item.title: REVIEW: Ugreen NASync DXP4800 GT Review: This Four-Bay NAS Punches Above Its Price
item.description:
Source: PCMag
With a peak potential storage capacity of 144TB, two high-speed LAN connections, and a variety of useful I/O ports, the Ugreen DXP4800 GT is an ideal network attached storage (NAS) device for multimedia enthusiasts, content creators, or anyone who requires a versatile data backup solution on a fast network. It’s a four-bay NAS that not only uses 10Gbps connectivity to deliver speedy file transfer performance but also offers an HDMI port, USB-A and USB-C ports, and an SD card slot, all of which make it easy to back up and share data. The DXP4800 GT doesn’t offer as many M.2 slots and multi-gig LAN ports as our previous top pick for four-bay NAS drives, the more-expensive Asustor Lockerstor 4 Gen 3 AS6804T ($1,299), nor can it match the number of downloadable apps that you get with the Lockerstor, but it is equipped with two M.2 slots, delivers similar performance, and at $699.99 is almost half the price. That earns it an Editors’ Choice nod for four-bay NAS devices. The DXP4800 GT has a gray aluminum enclosure with gold trim, measuring 10.1 by 7 by 7 inches (HWD). The front of the device is home to four lockable, removable drive sleds, a power button with an LED indicator, network and hard drive status LEDs, an SD card slot, and both Type-A and Type-C USB 3.2 Gen 2 ports. The sleds are tool-free if you’re using 3.5-inch drives, but they require screws (included) if you're using 2.5-inch drives. Two of the bays support 2.5-inch U.2 NVMe solid-state drives in lieu of 2.5-inch SATA hard drives. While many competitors offer M.2 slots for caching or extra storage, few offer U.2 compatibility. High-speed U.2 drives aren't much seen in consumer circles; they are mostly the preserve of servers in enterprises or data centers, or the highest-end workstations. Ugreen says this capability adds the option for enterprise-class endurance and sustained write performance in the main storage bay, which would be beneficial for housing active project files, virtual machine storage, or databases. As with nearly all NAS devices we review, storage drives are not included. The back panel is home to a pair of 10Gbps LAN jacks, an HDMI output, a second Type-A USB 3.2 Gen 2 port, two Type-A USB 2.0 ports, a power connector, a reset button, and a removable magnetic dust screen. Behind a removable panel on the bottom of the enclosure are two open M.2 slots and two RAM slots. The NAS comes with 8GB of DDR4 RAM, which is expandable to 64GB. Included in the box are two thermal pads for installing M.2 SSD modules, a LAN cable, an AC power adapter, drive screws, a screwdriver, and a user guide. The DXP4800 GT runs on a quad-core AMD Ryzen R2514 CPU. The above-mentioned 8GB of RAM is paired with 64GB of local eMMC flash memory. You can configure the drive bays for up to 144TB of storage; you'd get there using four 32TB SATA drives and two 8TB M.2 SSD drives. The enclosure supports RAID 0, RAID 1, RAID 5, RAID 6, RAID 10, JBOD, and Basic drive configurations. It also supports the EXT4 and BTRFS file systems. The DXP4800 GT uses the same UGOS Pro operating system as the Ugreen NASync DH4300 Plus that we recently reviewed. It can be controlled from a desktop using the web-based console or from a phone using the iOS or Android mobile app. When you first fire up the web console, you’ll see a Windows-like desktop screen with tiles labeled App Center, Control Panel, Files, Task Manager, Storage, and Logs. Additionally, you'll find tiles for the Recycle Bin and Support, where you can access the Information Center, contact support, and view the user guide. The App Center is where you go to download applications that let you use the NAS as a cloud server, a multimedia server, a surveillance center for your home cameras, a backup repository, and more. Ugreen currently offers 34 apps for this NAS, which pales in comparison to the Synology DiskStation DS425+ (more than 105 apps) and the Asustor AS6804T (more than 200 apps). To handle disk management tasks such as creating storage pools and volumes, formatting drives, and checking disk health, tap the Storage tile. Tap the Files tile to create and share folders, assign access permissions, and upload or download files. The Control Panel tile takes you to a screen where you can configure hardware and network settings, update firmware, enable SMB, FTP, and WebDAV file services, and grant user rights. The Task Manager tile opens a screen with charts of CPU, GPU, memory, and hard drive usage, and the Logs tile lets you view system events. Whenever you download an app, its tile will be added to the desktop for future access. Setting up the DXP4800 GT is easy. I installed four 10TB Seagate IronWolf 3.5-inch SATA drives (our standard test drives), connected the NAS and my desktop PC to a 2.5Gbps switch, and powered up the NAS. I then typed find.ugnas.com in my browser’s address bar, at which point the NAS was immediately identified. I tapped Connect, gave the NAS a name, and created an administrator account. Once the NAS rebooted, I tapped Start on the Welcome screen, created a storage pool and a volume, and selected RAID 5 with the BTRFS file system. This configuration yielded 27.2TB of storage under RAID 5's striping. After 13 hours, the drives were synchronized, and the installation was complete. The DXP4800 GT turned in excellent scores on our file transfer tests, in which we measure write and read speeds by moving a standard 4.9GB folder containing a mix of music, video, photo, and office document files back and forth between the NAS and the desktop PC. Its score of 284MBps on our write test was a close second to the Zettlab D4 (289MBps) and just a tad faster than the Asustor AS6804T (283Mbps). The Ugreen DH4300 Plus was the slowest, but not by much, with a score of 278MBps. On the read test, the DXP4800 GT managed 283MBps, which is identical to what we saw with the Asustor AS6804T and slightly faster than the Ugreen DH4300 Plus (278MBps). The Zettlab D4 led the pack with a score of 298MBps. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. I find a lot to like about the Ugreen NASync DXP4800 GT four-bay NAS. It’s an excellent performer and easy to set up, and it offers dual 10Gbps LAN ports and a host of high-speed USB ports. Additionally, it supports multiple storage types, including SATA drives big and small, M.2 and U.2 NVMe solid state drives, and SD cards. All this earns it an Editors’ Choice award for four-bay NAS devices. If you require an extra pair of multi-gig LAN ports, four M.2 slots, and a much wider variety of apps, consider the Asustor Lockerstor 4 Gen 3 AS6804T (also an Editors’ Choice winner), but note that at $1,299, it’s significantly more expensive. I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: REVIEW: Bambu Lab H3C 3D printer review: A nine-tool monster
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The Bambu Lab H3C is an excellent nine-tool 3D printer that printed everything we could throw at it. Whether you want nine-color PLA models, mix and match engineering filaments, or crazy squishable TPU shoes in a riot of color, this machine is a beast. If you don’t have low ceilings or a fear of step ladders, the H3C might be the only printer you’ll ever need. - +Works with multiple materials and nozzle sizes in the same print - -Really, really tall (over four feet) Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. The Bambu Lab H3C is the printer we’ve been waiting for: a true Bambu tool changer. It has nine “Swaptek” tools that use a technology similar to the H2C Vortek rack, except each nozzle is built into a lightweight, hardwired tool with a dedicated filament path. The H3C is Bambu’s fastest multicolor 3D printer, and though it reduces waste, it does not eliminate it. The H3C comes with a surprising “old school” technology: the ability to print 2.85mm filament. This is in response to China’s increasing fascination with 3D-printed shoes made with a wide variety of squishy TPU. Bambu sent along a few spools of their new super soft 75A TPU to show off, and it does make for comfy footwear. Each unit comes with one special 2.85mm tool as a standard feature, though you can buy a “normal” 1.75mm tool for $59 if you’re not into the novelty of phat filament. You will also be able to add cutting, drawing, embossing, and foil transfer tools to the system. These were not available at the time of review, but we’ve seen these accessories on the H2D and A2L. The 3D printer will NOT come with a laser variant. Bambu is checking off yet another item from the user wish list: the ability to print with more than one nozzle size. Because this is more of a software upgrade, you’ll also gain the ability to mix nozzles with Bambu’s other dual nozzle systems: the H2D, H2C, and X2D. The H2D will get the ability first, and the other printers will be updated by March. The H3C has a 330 x 320 x 325mm build volume (the same as the H2C) and a massive “AMS” type module perched atop the main unit that holds nine spools. This gives it a somewhat towering mushroom shape that’s over three feet tall. It did not fit on my studio counter, which is a standard-sized IKEA kitchen countertop with a filament rack three feet off the surface. When we parked it on my industrial-grade shelving unit next to the H2D, even my 6’4” husband needed a step stool to load filament. Bambu was prepared for this problem and created a special rolling cart for the machine to make it more accessible. This is the first time the company has offered custom furniture for one of their printers and is an optional purchase that I highly recommend. All nine tools are integrated into the bottom of the AMS 3H, which means the H3C only comes as a nine-tool 3D printer. There is no such thing as a single-color H3C. If nine colors aren’t enough for you, the printer can be hooked up to as many as four “normal” AMS units with the help of an optional buffer. Unfortunately, all outside AMS units need to run through the 5th tool slot, so you will lose the purge-free perk of the H3C. The AMS 3H does not have motorized rollers, as retraction is unneeded on a tool changer. Seven of the slots have a TPU bypass, something we first saw on the single spool AMS HT. Two of the slots are nestled within an interior chamber for drying at up to 85°C. Though you can only dry two spools in the AMS 3H, you can run the dryer while printing, as it has its own power supply. The sealed dryer does not “leak” enough heat to dry the rest of the chamber…we checked. But that also means you don’t have to worry about the dryer melting a spool of PLA left in a nearby slot. The FlexFeed extruder mounted on the toolhead is amazing. It can self-adjust to handle normal 1.75mm PLA or expand to push 2.85mm TPU quickly and without issue. The Bambu Lab H3C comes standard with eight .4mm nozzles for 1.75mm filament and one .4mm nozzle for 2.85mm filament. The nozzles are held in place with three screws and are pretty easy to swap out. You do need an entirely separate tool (with larger openings) for the 2.85mm filament. Because the H3C can print with multiple nozzle sizes, you could leave one or more tools dedicated to .2, .6, or .8 nozzle sizes if that fits your workflow. For example, slots 6 and 8 are located inside the dryer and have a TPU bypass. You could dedicate a .6mm nozzle to these tools to better handle TPU, something like PA CF, which both benefit from toasty dry filament and an extra-wide nozzle. All nozzles for the H3C are hardened steel (HRC 55+) by default. My H3C did have some pre-launch issues and is running Beta firmware that was updated several times during the review. The printer developed an annoying clicking sound coming from the left-side stepper motor, and one of the tools has a tendency to tangle and catch on the other Bowden tubes, causing it to dismount unexpectedly – and annoyingly – during long multicolor prints. I printed a few TPU spacers to try and solve this problem without much success as of yet. The Bambu Lab H3C is launching with a retail price starting at $2,499 for all nine tools (eight standard 1.75mm and one 2.85mm). This is only $100 more than the launch price of the H2C. Additional tools and nozzle sizes will be available, though we do not have all the pricing at this time. A bundle that includes the Bambu Station (rolling cart) starts at $2,799. This makes the machine a bit on the spendy side, but for a helmet-class, honest-to-goodness tool changer with Bambu Lab’s ease of use, this 3D printer has earned its place on our Best 3D Printer of 2026 list. The Bambu Lab H3C comes with a toolkit and the cables needed to assemble your 3D printer, as well as a few spare parts. The printer is preloaded with files, including a scraper that you can build yourself with the included parts. There’s also a quick start guide for both the base unit and the AMS 3H. For the review, Bambu Lab provided spare printer tools for both 1.75mm and 2.85mm filaments, as well as several spools of PLA Palette and 2.85mm TPU 75A. We also received a Bambu Station for the review. The H3C is an incredible piece of hardware. The Swaptek system has nine tools, each with its own filament path, heater, and hardened steel nozzle. The FlexFeed extruder has cooling and everything else. Each nozzle stays loaded and is preheated for lightning-fast filament swaps. I clocked it at six seconds from printing one color to printing the next. The tools and nozzles come in both 1.75 mm and 2.85 mm filament sizes. Each tool has a nozzle attached by three screws, which can be swapped with different sizes. The H3C ships with one 2.85mm tool, but you have the option to purchase more tools if you want to customize your configuration. Though not ready at the time of this review, Bambu Lab will be offering tools for cutting, drawing, debossing, and foil transfer at a later date. The tools dock on a front-mounted rack that retracts, allowing the build plate to be viewed from the front of the printer. This is a not-so-subtle jab at Prusa’s INDX, which has tools mounted to a fixed rack that one must peer through to see the first layer printing. It adds a layer of unneeded complexity, but it also looks pretty cool in action. The photo below shows all nine tools lowered, using a maintenance setting. Normally, only one tool lowers at a time while in use. Unlike previous Bambu Lab 3D printers, the AMS is required, not optional. Instead of a box that can be parked here or there, the AMS 3H is designed to screw into the top of the H3C. The plastic sides have a weird organic shape, but are actually quite practical – hidden side panels pop out for maintenance, allowing you to reach into the machine. The massive lid can be propped open, which is good because it’s most likely going to be over your head. The tools ship attached to the bottom of the AMS. Though the H3C has the same build volume, and the same length and width as the H2 line, it is doubtful that an H2 can be upgraded to an H3C by simply plopping an AMS 3H on top of an older machine. The AMS 3H has a separate chamber with a magnetically attached lid covering slots 6 and 8, which can dry filament at up to 85°C. All filament slots except 2 and 4 can bypass the AMS feeders through a hole in the bottom to directly feed TPU to the tools. The spool slots are numbered in a zigzag method, with 2,4,6 and 8 on the back row and 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 on the front. All the filament feeders are in the middle of the two rows, with the even-numbered spools feeding forward like always, and the odd spools feeding backward. It can get a bit complicated if you’re not using Bambu-branded filament with RFID tags. Being on the short side, I have to use a step stool to see the feeders. The body of the Bambu Lab H3C looks similar to the rest of the H series except for the toolhead. The Flexfeed extruder can adjust automatically to push multiple filament widths and does well with some of the softest TPU I’ve tried. The H3C has active chamber heating, up to 65°C, goes to 350°C at the hot end and 120°C on the bed, which makes printing PPA and PPS, nylons, ABS, and ASA easy. For the smellier filaments, it has active carbon and HEPA filtration. The ventilation is sufficient to run lower-temperature filaments like PLA with the printer’s door closed. The printer has an excellent camera that is used for AI detection on prints and can be monitored from the Bambu Handy app as well as the device page of Bambu Slicer. The camera can also capture time-lapses of prints when a USB stick is inserted in the slot behind the touch screen. The Bambu Lab H3C has a footprint similar to the other H series printers but does require space on both sides to access the side panels of the AMS 3H. With the top-mounted AMS and the space required for the tool wiring and Bowden tubes, the Bambu Lab H3C requires a total of 1306 mm in height (over four feet) to operate comfortably. When resting on a standard-height counter or the 3ft tall racks we normally use for our printers, I needed a small ladder to reach the rear spools in the AMS 3H. Even my husband, who is 6’4,” had to stretch to reach the back. Shortly after I had the printer set up, I received the Bambu Station, which, at 23.5 inches tall on its wheels, is a great solution for keeping this printer in reach. If you don’t have a shelf or table the height of a coffee table, I recommend getting one. Bambu is also introducing a companion E1 Air Purifier that syncs with the H3C and activates when you start a print job. We did not receive an E1 to test, and we’re not sure if the air cleaner will be offered as a standalone product. It is part of the premium $3,049 combo that includes the printer, rolling cart, and several spools of filament. The Bambu Lab H3C arrives in two large assemblies: the main printer and all the things attached to the AMS 3H. After removing the packing material, zip ties holding the tool head in place, four screws holding the bed in place, and two retainers holding the rack in place, the AMS 3H can be hefted on top of the base unit. This is best done while the unit is on the floor or at least somewhere with a bunch of overhead clearance. The touch screen attaches to the base unit without tools, and the ribbon cable is just long enough to reach the back of the screen. The nine tools have to be manually placed in the front rack, which takes some time until you learn how they attach. At least one needed to be attached once the printer was powered up. The AMS 3H has its own power cord for the heater and a cable connecting it to the base. There are preinstalled screws to attach the Base unit to the AMS 3H, but I left these unused since removing the front panel requires tipping the AMS 3H back a bit. The Bambu Lab H3C performs a bed level as part of its initial calibration suite and again before each print. This works flawlessly in practice. When using non-TPU 1.75mm filament, the AMS 3H loads filament just like a regular AMS. Filament is inserted into the feeder, which automatically pulls it into the toolhead when that tool is selected. The RFID tag on Bambu Lab branded filament will automatically enter the filament type and color. Other filament brands need to be entered manually into the printer via the touchscreen. The AMS 3H does not have powered rollers to retract the filament. You will need to select Unload from the filament screen, and the printer will cut the filament and retract it from the tool head. You will need to manually pull the filament out the rest of the way. 2.85mm filament and softer TPU will need to be manually fed through a port on the bottom of the AMS 3H. All filament slots except 2 and 4 have this port. The filament bypasses the tubing to feed directly into the tools. The standard Bowden tube must be removed from the tool and inserted into a holder on the side. For 1.75mm TPU, a small piece of Bowden tube is inserted into the top of the tool to help feed the filament correctly. 2.85mm filament can be inserted directly into the tool. Once inserted, filament using the bypass must be loaded manually. Preparing Files / Software for Bambu Lab H3C Bambu Studio, based on PrusaSlicer and its forbear, is one of the best slicers out there. Working seamlessly with the printer for filament mapping, control, monitoring, and access to all of the files on Makerworld, it is a joy to use. The H3C is a much faster machine than its predecessors because it does not need to reel filament back and forth from the AMS. However, it still uses a purge tower, which can waste a bit of time and filament. It only takes about six seconds to swap tools, which is quite remarkable. The H3C did not come with filament samples, but Bambu Lab did send along several spools of PLA Palette and spools of 2.85 75A TPU to try. You’re going to need a bunch of filament for this beast, so check out our list of best filaments for 3D printing for suggestions. To get the measure of the Bambu Lab H3C, I loaded up one of my favorite prints, a steampunk dragon by the designer Cinderwing 3D. I had previously printed it in eight PLA colors using two AMS modules on an Anycubic Kobra 3 Max, which is a bed slinger. That first print took 37 hours and 28 minutes and wasted 267g of filament in poop and purge. Using a .2mm layer height and an average print speed of 140mm/s, the H3C cut that time down to a bit less than 24 hours, and only wasted 68g in its purge tower. The print quality is excellent, and all the colors came out clean. The main color is Prusa Pearl Mouse, Polymaker Panchroma Silver, and black, white, magenta, yellow, and cyan from Bambu’s new Palette PLA, which is actually designed for color mixing. Eight colors were not enough. I swapped out the 2.85mm tool with the spare 1.75mm tool and printed a nine-color Princess Donut and Mongo from Dungeon Crawler Carl (my latest obsession). I have been using this print to test out other tool changers for a future comparison. The print came out fantastic, with super shiny silks and clean color transitions. I had to “hand paint” this in Bambu Slicer, which took a bit of time. The teeth on the print are a bit shaky, but that is due to the insane amount of support this model required. This printed in 15 hours and 12 minutes, with a 152.6-gram prime tower, using a .2mm layer height and default settings. For comparison, the same print with the same settings but only 5 colors on the H2C took 24 hours and 44 minutes and used 111.4grams on its prime tower. The Prusa INDX took a similar amount of time (15 hours and 38 minutes) to run the same print in 8 colors, but only needed to waste 24grams of prime purge. Filaments: The Bambu Lab H3C is one of the best printers I’ve tested for printing TPU. The AMS 3H bypass ports require a tiny bit of set up, but they are much better than dealing with an external spool holder. With nine slots at my disposal, I can always have a spool of TPU ready to go. My first TPU print was a strap hinge that combines normal 95A TPU with stiff PLA brackets. The designer wove the two filaments together manually, though you can make your own hinges flexible by using “beam interlocking” in the slicer. I printed this in Polymaker red PLA and Polymaker red TPU 95A and the hinge is extremely strong. Printed with a .2mm layer height and running at an average speed of 115 mm/s the print completed in just over an hour. I was excited to try the 2.85mm 75A TPU that Bambu Lab sent, and it did not disappoint. The 2.85mm nozzle comes preset to run filament directly from the bypass and just requires manual loading. This is the softest TPU I’ve ever run, and the FlexFeed extruder handled it perfectly. I first ran the wrist rest from the printer’s memory using Bambu Lab’s green 75A TPU. The print took 50 minutes to run, used only 20g of filament, and is very squishy. I used the same filament and printed some tires for an RC project I’m working on. Using a .2mm layer height and an average print speed of 75mm/s the tires took 57 minutes per set of two. They look nice and are super squishy. They only have 2 walls and 7% concentric infill, so they are extremely lightweight. For ABS, I ran a two-color Magic 8-ball-style D20. Dice Studio lets you print custom dice with numbers or text and export it as a 3mf file ready to print. This is printed in Ionized Cobalt Black Matte ABS and Natural Matte ABS from Fusion Filaments. The print was very nice, with just a little roughness on the overhangs on the very bottom of the die, and a little roughness on the text where it becomes very small. To really test out the heated chamber, I used a filament I struggle with: PA6 GF. I printed a Twist Lock Container using grey PA6 GF from Sunlu. I ran it with 3 walls and a .2mm layer height at an average speed of 140mm/s. The print took nearly 6 hours to complete. The result is a nearly indestructible canister that looks good too. The H3C is quite the multimaterial powerhouse and handles every material equally well. I don’t own any filament that it can’t print well, from soft TPU to PPS. Multiple nozzle sizes and multiple filament sizes can all be used together, and you’ve got nine places to put it all. Unless you need a print farm, I can’t really see the need for a different printer. This is a one-stop shop. With a retail price of $2,499 for the H3C Tool Changer, this is a printer to definitely put on your wish list. In fact, I’m so impressed with the tool changer aspect, I keep forgetting that it’s also a helmet-class printer, which makes this machine capable of handling nearly any print you need to create. If the Bambu Lab H3C seems out of reach, you can also check out last year’s Bambu Lab H2C, which is no slouch at multimaterial and has the same build volume. It’s currently on sale for $1,899 with a four-color AMS combo. The Snapmaker U1 is the most affordable tool changer we like on the market right now, and though it is smaller and only four-color, the $699 Black Friday price tag is very tempting. And of course, we have the Prusa CORE One INDX eight-color machine for those who want to keep their printers off the cloud, currently retailing at $1,949 as a kit.

item.title: REVIEW: CZUR ET Max Review: Digitizing Books? This Scanner's a Spine-Saver
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The CZUR ET Max is an overhead scanner that’s bundled with customized software designed to make scanning entire books as painless and efficient as possible. For books that can’t lie flat on a flatbed scanner, an overhead scanner may be the only viable solution. This model includes curve-flattening software tools that correct curved or skewed pages, a module with side-mounted lights that reduces glare and reflections, OCR functionality for converting scanned text to searchable text, and a built-in HDMI port for sending real-time audio and video output to an external display. It’s best to think of the ET Max as a highly specialized scanner. For loose pages, a sheetfed document scanner would be faster and easier to use, and it would provide superior results. For books that can lay flat on a glass platen, a flatbed scanner could successfully tackle the job—as long as you’re not scanning too many pages. However, for bound books, spiral notebooks, periodicals, and fragile documents that a sheetfed or flatbed scanner can't easily handle, an overhead scanner can be the better choice. And the ET Max is the best one that we’ve seen so far. It replaces the old CZUR ET24 Pro as our Editors' Choice pick for a professional-grade overhead scanner. The ET Max arrives in a well-protected box that includes a large overhanging stand with a built-in camera sensor, a detachable side-lights module, a large black work mat, a USB hand control, a USB foot pedal, two plastic finger cots, a USB cable, and a power adapter. The black work mat measures 20.9 inches by 15.8 inches. An indentation on one side of the mat allows the stand to reach in about 0.8 inch. Even with that indentation, the stand will protrude about 5.75 inches out from the mat. And the stand itself is about 15.5 inches tall. I mention all this because this unit is wider, deeper, and taller than your typical sheetfed or flatbed scanner. In other words, you may want to measure before deciding whether the ET Max is a good fit for your workspace. You need a large work area because the ET Max resembles a top-mounted view camera more than a traditional scanner, even though it functions like one. With most scanners, either the document moves in relation to the sensor (think of a page being pulled in and scanned by a sheetfed scanner), or the sensor moves in relation to the document (think of a flatbed’s sensor passing back and forth beneath a stationary page). With an overhead scanner such as the ET Max, nothing moves—the lens is far enough away to capture everything at once. It’s like a specialized camera with a fixed lens optimized for a particular distance and set of dimensions. This kind of setup is especially well suited for repetitive tasks, such as scanning books. You can scan books with a flatbed scanner, but it takes longer between pages, as you have to lift the book and reposition it after each scan. For longer books, those intervals can add up to a significant amount of time. Another advantage of an overhead scanner like the ET Max is its ability to work with books that aren’t perfectly flat. Unless you’re willing to break a book’s binding, it can be very difficult to get a satisfactory scan from a bound book using a flatbed scanner. Either you’ll damage the book’s binding, or the facing pages will appear curved toward the center of the scan. With an overhead scanner, that’s less of an issue because the focus doesn’t need to be as tight. Plus, the scanner might include software that can digitally correct the problem. And with the ET Max, you can use the supplied finger cots to press down on the facing pages to help minimize the curvature. Why not just use an overhead scanner for all your scanning needs? Here we come to the two main disadvantages of this kind of scanner, and why they’re mostly a niche category. The first disadvantage is the lack of an automatic document feeder (ADF). For most kinds of loose documents, it’s much faster and easier to use a document scanner or the built-in scanner on an AIO printer. It’s when you’re trying to digitize bound books, spiral notebooks, periodicals, or fragile documents that you should consider an overhead scanner. The second disadvantage is the reduced resolution. Most document scanners have an optical resolution of 600dpi. The ET Max has a rating of 410dpi, a significant increase over the previous model, the ET24 Pro. The ET Max has a 38-megapixel sensor, while the ET24 Pro has a smaller 24-megapixel sensor that gives it a more limited 320dpi. Like the ET24 Pro, the IRIScan Desk 7 Business also has a 24-megapixel sensor, though IRIS lists it as having a 600dpi resolution. That 600dpi is a software-interpolated resolution, which isn’t directly comparable to the optical (or native) resolutions that CZUR lists for its models. If you’re scanning books that consist entirely of text, the dpi count may not matter much, as long as the error rate from the included OCR software is low enough for your needs. If you’re scanning books with a lot of images, though, the dpi rating may be more of an issue for you. Keep in mind that graphics scanned with an overhead scanner will likely not be as sharp as those from a traditional sheetfed or flatbed scanner. On the other hand, the ET Max can scan open books or documents up to 18.9 by 14.2 inches. It would take an unusually large sheetfed or flatbed scanner to accommodate books or documents of that size. The ET Max includes a CD-ROM disc with the necessary software and drivers. If you're like most people in 2026 and your computer doesn’t have a CD-ROM drive, you can download the software installer using the link that’s listed in the printed setup guide. The software installer is compatible with Windows XP, 7, 8, 10, and 11; Macs (both Apple M-series and Intel silicon-based); and Linux. Your CPU must be an Intel Core i7 (8th generation or later) or an AMD Ryzen (7th generation or later). You’ll also need at least 8GB of RAM, though 16GB is recommended. After downloading and initially running the software, you’ll be asked to input the serial number that’s affixed to the bottom of the unit. Once that’s done, you can continue on with the software installation. On my Windows PC testbed, I ended up with just two apps: a CZUR Scanner app, and an Uninstall CZUR Scanner app. That's fewer than many competing scanners offer, but the CZUR Scanner app is comprehensive, as I'll discuss below. On the hardware side, you’ll need to attach the provided USB cable to both the scanner and your computer. Plug either the hand control or the foot pedal into the scanner’s available USB port at the back of the base, and spread out the black work mat, using the notched gap in the mat to align the scanner so it overhangs the mat. You can then turn on the ET Max using the power switch on its base's back. The main overhead laser lamps should come on automatically. If they don’t, you can press the button on the stand with the lightbulb icon. If you’ll be scanning magazines, glossy books, coated paper, or other reflective materials, you should also attach and switch on the side-lights module. It has a touch-sensitive switch, so it’s easy to turn on and off. One particularly welcome feature on the ET Max is the 2.5-inch color LCD at the end of the scanner’s head. You’ll want to use it to see if the mat covers the entire screen. If not, you’ll need to reposition the mat to keep extraneous content from peeking in on any of the four sides. The screen can also serve as a visual aid for centering your book or document onto the mat. And just below the screen, you’ll see three small lights: a video-recording indicator light, a scan indicator light, and a power indicator light. CZUR suggests that you avoid scanning near a window or under overhead lighting. Excessively bright ambient lighting can overwhelm the built-in laser lamps and adversely affect scanning results. The company also suggests that when scanning larger projects such as books or multiple documents, you use the foot pedal in conjunction with the computer screen to make the process more efficient. The CZUR Scanner app lets you choose between Flat Single Page and Facing Pages modes. The Flat Single Page mode is, predictably, for single pages or single sheets of paper, where no curvature correction is needed. The Facing Pages mode is for bound books or bound sheets of paper. This is where the software's curvature correction routines are activated. The software does a decent job of automatically recognizing the edges of the paper, cropping or tilting pages when necessary, and flattening the curves characteristic of facing pages in bound books. That said, it does help if the curves aren’t too extreme. To help you alleviate that, the ET Max includes two yellow finger cots. You use them to press down on the blank spaces of the facing pages as you scan the pages using the foot pedal. The finger cots can then be automatically removed from the scan by the software. You won’t need to use the cots unless a significant amount of curvature is involved. Precisely positioning your book for the Facing Pages mode is also relatively simple. The software will show you an orange vertical line that runs parallel to the border between the two facing pages. You can use that orange line to help you align the center of the book in relation to the scanner’s camera. The software can also automatically detect when you’ve turned to a new page and adjust for any slight deviation. With so much being handled automatically by the software, all you really need to do is repeatedly press the foot pedal and turn the pages carefully enough that you don’t accidentally reposition the book. It’s easy to get into a rhythm if you’re trying to scan an entire book or long article. After you’ve scanned all the pages, you can use the app to rotate or crop the results, erase any handwritten notes, or embed a watermark or logo. Many of the edit tools can also be applied to multiple pages at a time, including edge cropping, hole filling, handwriting erase, and standardization (such as for scaling or background color processing). These are the kinds of tools that you may not find with a sheetfed or flatbed scanner. They’re a welcome addition for anyone who has to spend hours at a stretch scanning books or fragile documents. Once you have all the pages just the way you want them, you can save the results to a variety of file formats. The software uses optical character recognition (OCR) technology to convert your scanned text to a Word, Excel, or searchable PDF file. If OCR processing isn’t needed, you can save your scanned results to a non-searchable PDF, TXT, TIFF, PNG, or BMP file. You can also print your scans directly from within the CZUR Scanner app. Like the ET24 Pro, the ET Max has a built-in HDMI port, allowing it to be used as a presentation device. How does that work? First, make sure the unit is connected to an AC power supply and not connected to a computer via a USB cable. Next, you attach an HDMI cable (not included) to both the ET Max and an HDMI-compatible projector, television, or electronic whiteboard. Now, when you turn on the ET Max, it will automatically enter its Visual Presenter mode. The scanner's head has a built-in microphone you can speak into during the presentation. And the base unit has buttons you can use to zoom in or out on the display image, which can be of anything you can fit onto the black mat. CZUR gives the ET Max a speed rating of 1.5 seconds per scan. The ET24 Pro has that same speed rating, while the IRIScan Desk 7 Business has an even faster rating of just 1 second per scan. When converted to the pages-per-minute (ppm) standard used for document scanners, the ET Max’s 1.5 seconds per scan works out to a respectable 40ppm. That’s fast enough to match some currently available document scanners. The difference, of course, is that the ET Max is a manual scanner. It can automatically sense a new page and readjust the camera amazingly fast, but you’re the one who has to turn the pages without disrupting the process. After some trial and error, I was able to reach a rate of 1.9 seconds per scan, which works out to be 31.6ppm. In theory, that would allow me to scan a 320-page book in about 10 minutes. That pace is probably par for the course, as CZUR advertises that you can “scan a 300-page book in 10 minutes with ease.” In real life, it may not be worth the strain of maintaining top speed, as keeping up that pace for an extended period (even 10 minutes!) can be tiring. Plus, the process gets monotonous if you’re scanning hundreds of pages in one sitting. This is a much more labor-intensive procedure than with a document scanner. What about scan quality? Almost any document scanner can convert printed pages to error-free, editable text down to 6 points in both our Arial (sans-serif) and Times New Roman (serif) font tests. Even though this is not a document scanner, the ET Max did meet that standard. It converted printed pages to error-free, editable text down to 6-point type in both our Arial (sans-serif) and Times New Roman (serif) font tests. While business documents will rarely have text that’s smaller than 10 points, you may find some small books with text that’s smaller than 10 points. Having a 6-point accuracy could come in handy in that situation. The quality of the scanned graphics didn’t quite match that of a typical document scanner. As mentioned previously, while greatly improved compared with earlier models, the ET Max’s scan resolution still falls short of document-scanner standards. That’s not to say that the results will be unacceptable. There may be a slight reduction in sharpness, especially in areas that have fine detail. And the colors may be less accurate when compared with the original. If those things are critical, you might consider using a flatbed scanner, at least for specific pages or sections that need extra clarity. Overall, though, the quality may be close enough that most people wouldn’t notice. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. If you’re in need of a professional-quality overhead scanner, the CZUR ET Max has refined the category to a remarkable degree. It has a high-resolution sensor that approaches the sharpness and detail that you would find with a sheetfed or flatbed scanner, which is no small feat. The software app can virtually flatten the curved pages of an open book and automatically split double pages into two. It includes finger cots that let you hold down stubborn pages, along with software that efficiently erases the cots from the scans. And it throws in an HDMI-compatible presenter mode that lets you use the device as a modern-day overhead projector. Add this all together, and the ET Max is our Editors' Choice winner for the best professional-grade overhead scanner. Who should buy an ET Max? It’s a good pick for small and midsize offices, presenters, teachers, and others in need of its very specific talents. For smaller projects, a sheetfed or flatbed scanner might be a better choice, assuming the book or document fits within their capabilities. However, for bound books or even unbound books with hundreds of pages, the ET Max’s specialized tools make it an easy recommendation for what might otherwise be a near-impossible task. At PCMag, my focus is on printers and scanners. I started out way back in 1988 at Compute!, which still had a section of the magazine devoted to type-in programs. Since then, I’ve written more than 1,000 articles for a variety of publications, including Architectural Record, Attaché, CNET, COMDEX Daily, Computer Shopper, Digital Cinema Report, Film & Video, Hemispheres, The Leica Camera Blog, Maximum PC, Omni, PC Magazine, PC World, Sky, StudioDaily, US Airways Magazine, and ZDNET. My interest in printers stems from my interest in digital photography. Ten of my photos were featured in a solo exhibition at the Leica Store at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas. Titled “Monochrome Vegas,” the large photo prints were displayed there for more than a year. I’m also interested in technology-based music. I’ve created a large number of music videos that combine improvised music with computer graphics. You can view my photography at protozoid.com and my music videos on my YouTube channel.

item.title: REVIEW: Dungeons & Dragons’ World of Warcraft module might be perfect
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Universes Beyond has finally leapt from Magic: The Gathering and into Wizards of the Coast’s other hugely popular game, Dungeons & Dragons, with the release of its World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion — a 256-page book detailing precisely how the planet of Azeroth should be adapted into the most popular tabletop RPG. I’ve spent the last couple of weeks devouring this new book, and while I’ll admit to already being a fan of Universes Beyond — I think it has done an amazing job of introducing my favorite trading card game to complete newcomers, and I have hopes it’ll do the same for D&D — whether you’re in my camp, or you’re someone who would rather keep your game worlds isolated, I think you’ll struggle to find complaints with this module. Of course the book heavily focuses on the WoW-ness of the additions it makes to the TTRPG, yet so many of the new races, subclasses, monsters, and other rules could easily slot into any campaign setting. And if you need a little extra nudge, this book includes the long-awaited refresh of some fan-favorite subclasses which had yet to receive their post-2024 update (like the Swashbuckler Rogue and Way of the Drunken Master Monk, renamed to Warrior of Mystic Brews). Though perhaps best of all, none of this excellent new content will destroy your bank balance. The Gameplay Expansion costs $59.99 / £49.99 / AU$84.99, which, while at the higher end of what D&D books sell for, feels like a reasonable price considering the amount here for players and Dungeon Masters. Plus, third-party retailers are sure to sell you this expansion for less than MSRP, especially during sales periods when D&D books are known to get a price cut. My only disappointment is that I feel it’s not the most newcomer-friendly if you’re looking to be the Dungeon Master — the person who has to run the games. Just a quick one-shot adventure would do the trick to get the ball rolling, but as is, I’d suggest the DM is someone with D&D experience. Which is a shame considering Universes Beyond’s new-player appeal. That said, I think this expansion is excellent no matter your affinity for WoW, but if you’re still unsure whether you should grab the World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion for Dungeons & Dragons, let me explain a little more why I love it. Let’s begin where this book does: Chapter 1: Character Classes. Every class in Dungeons & Dragons features in this World of Warcraft expansion to give players a guide for how the TTRPG can be adapted to fit the champions Azeroth locals will be familiar with. Admittedly, some get more attention than others, but what I loved to read was that every class gets at least something new — rather than some being ignored entirely like with other recent expansions. For those on the shorter end of the stick — Druids, Wizards, Fighters, Warlocks, and Rangers (though they’re a special case I’ll get back to later) — this means just some new spells, Battle Master maneuvers, or Eldritch Invocations. Though I’m not complaining after reading through their new tools. Conjuration-focused Warlocks will love the Expendable Minions invocation, which turns downed minions into healing for you or an ally, while the new version of Mass Polymorph feels like a hilariously perfect way for a more chaotic Wizard to dispatch a surrounding army — transforming any number of terrifying foes into harmless goats. You’ll also notice these classes, and all others, have simple guides to follow for what spells and feature choices to make so that the D&D class feels most like the World of Warcraft specializations. Some class names have changed too. Wizard is Mage, Fighter is Warrior, and Rangers are Hunters (I’ll highlight other class name variations as we go). One step above are Monks, Paladins, Clerics (Priests), Rogues, and Barbarians (Shamans), who all get a new subclass or two, or at least a revised version of a subclass, yet to be updated since the 2024 rules update. In that latter camp are the Swashbuckler Rogue and Drunken Master Monk, which has been renamed Warrior of Mystic Brews. As with other post-2024 rules update refreshes, these subclasses feel very familiar, though there are some mechanical tweaks here and there to better balance the player option against the other choices you could make — or, in the case of Warrior of Mystic Brews, make the subclass feel like a more distinct option in your repertoire. The brand-new subclasses steal the show to some extent because of their freshness, and I’m desperate to play an Oath of the Holy Paladin in my next campaign. This version of the knight is far more focused on healing than fighting — fulfilling a more supportive tank role; however, I still wouldn’t want to get struck by its Divine Smite. Finally, circling back on the Ranger’s ‘special case,’ you’ll find three so-called Hero Classes — the Death Knight, Demon Hunter, and Evoker. This never-before-seen flavor of character option is a sort of subclass, but rather than building on the existing class’s base, they tear down and rebuild some core aspects (something subclasses don’t tend to do). For example, the Oath of the Ebon Blade Death Knight takes away the Paladin’s healing Lay on Hands and turns it into a damaging Death Coil, and transforms the heavenly Divine Smite into a demonic Runic Smite. Calling them ‘Hero Classes’ does perhaps suggest a level of superiority; however, I haven’t necessarily felt that from the options present. These don’t feel like the new best way to play a class, merely an alternative way. The Hero Class designation just denotes that there’s a layer of complexity because the core class is altered — though I found the World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion’s guide very easy to follow, and I expect newcomers won’t struggle to build one of these three options if they follow it. Characters are more than their class, however. Unfortunately, the World of Warcraft expansion doesn’t provide us with any new Backgrounds — pre-adventure origins which determine the starting skills of the player’s character — but there is a wide selection of fantastical races to select from, and various WoW factions for their party members to develop an affiliation with. Much like classes, if there is an existing Dungeons & Dragons native — such as Dwarves or Elves — you’re asked to lift the rules from the Player’s Handbook, but races or variants of races that exist only in WoW are given bespoke traits. The monastic Pandaren can use their Inner Peace to recover more health when resting, and leave foes quaking after an attack, while Dracthyr can use their wings to glide — taking no falling damage if the drop is under 100ft, and being able to travel horizontally as they plummet. Of course, there are also a few pages spared for mounts and creature companions — iconic World of Warcraft pets that you can ride into battle, or which offer some small buff if your friendship with them is high enough. Factions are lifted wholesale. The Alliance and the Horde (and their respective subfactions) take center stage, but there are other groups a party may prefer to build a relationship with. There are some mechanical advantages to building renown with various factions, but they’re generally a narrative device — Dungeon Masters have a reliable quest giver in the form of friendly faction leaders; they could lock greater quest progression behind first gaining the trust of a new faction, or force players into a strained truce with rival factions to work together to achieve some greater goal (requiring careful role-playing scenarios to ensure the two sides don’t resume their hostilities). I’ll get back to the toys and tools this Gameplay Expansion affords DMs, but finishing things off on the players' side, we need to talk about Professions. Professions expand the basic crafting rules from the 2024 Player’s Handbook and Dungeon Master’s Guide by providing players specific guidance on how to develop their character’s foraging and item-making skills — and how to take advantage of these abilities. For parties who spend a lot of time among civilisation, these skills aren’t going to change their games very much, I expect, but if you’re planning a campaign which ventures deep into the wilderness (which I now am after being inspired by these rules), they’ll provide a vital way for the group to replenish and upgrade their gear. The basic idea is that crafted items and foraged resources are given specific values based on their rarity and where they were found. Collect enough resources, and you can create an item that’s worth as much as the combined value of the resources you’re using — provided they’re of the appropriate type, i.e., foraged plants and animal viscera are perfect for potions, while mined ores and animal skins are used for weapons and armour. The rulebook stays away from generating specific recipes outside one or two examples, but it encourages DMs to bring the crafting system to life within their game world. This could involve requiring specific quantities of specific resources rather than merely generic value — i.e., a potion of waterbreathing needing five pieces of common stranglekelp, and two vials of oil extracted from the rare blackmouth fish rather than merely 100GP of parts — or turning getting a specific rare resource into a side quest — such as a Staff of Fire requiring a ruby plundered from an adult dragon’s horde, or tracking down an expert blacksmith if crafting a magic sword for the first time. Though the rulebook encourages DMs and players to not turn their D&D adventure into a grinding slog. Repetitive actions are boring, and constantly diverting attention away from the main quest might derail the campaign into one about crafting gear with no real purpose behind the item making. Even if collecting enough of a resource might take a character a week to do in-game, this could be handled with just a couple of die rolls and only take a few minutes of real-world time — with that week either using up the character’s downtime allotment or impacting the ongoing quest if there are time-sensitive elements. The second half of the book is dedicated to describing the world of Azeroth. It takes you through the planet’s mythology, a brief history, and its geography — providing a quick description of key locations — before delving into a selection of iconic dungeons you could explore on your adventures, and a bestiary of foes you could face off against. It’s very much a section dedicated to the Dungeon Master, the ‘player’ who runs the whole game for the party. Providing them with many of the tools they’ll need to manage an engaging campaign, or one-shot for the group. Much like the rest of the book, it strikes a balance between in-depth information and leaving room for the DM’s creativity. And while it’s not the most relevant to players, I think it’s a smart idea that it’s included in this singular expansion rather than being a standalone product — making this WoW 5e release feel very approachable because you don’t need to decipher which selection of books you need; it’s just this one and the three core rulebooks (Player’s Handbook, Dungeon Master’s Guide, Monster Manual). As a more experienced DM, I love the more light-touch approach — it provides more freedom for me to adapt the Azeroth elements for my own campaigns on or off its world — however, I do think newer Dungeon Masters will struggle with the resources here. I understand that Dungeons & Dragons modules tend to lay things out alphabetically, but I think it would have been smarter to order the pre-made dungeons in challenge rating order so that it’s easier to find the noob-friendly expeditions. I also wish there was a more fleshed-out starter adventure that takes pre-made characters from level one to levels three or four, with guidance on how to manage running puzzles, combat encounters, and social interactions. Coming from Magic: The Gathering, I’ve seen how Universes Beyond excels as an onboarding tool for newer players, and for the most part this World of Warcraft expansion hits the mark. However, on the actual adventure-running side, without a proper, even just a quick one-shot to guide newer Dungeon Masters through the motions of running a game, I can see it being a struggle for complete newcomers to jump into their first TTRPG game. This one-shot would also simplify the resources you need out of the gate, because the premade character sheets and adventure could include any relevant details you’d find in the core rulebooks, like race traits and stat blocks. This reduces the barrier to entry to just this one World of Warcraft book to get into your first adventure, without removing the need to pick up the core rulebooks if you’re keen to play a full-on campaign. As it stands, I think the World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion for Dungeons & Dragons is mostly excellent. As someone with little affinity for this Universes Beyond IP, I’ve been pleasantly surprised by how much I have been inspired by its contents, and how excited I am to use its new player options and rules in future games. For D&D newcomers, this expansion is superb for players — the guides under each class for how to best build its WoW counterpart are a superb detail that should help remove the initial decision paralysis that can afflict newer players who aren’t 100% sure what they should choose — but I wish it offered more support to new DMs. Folks with some experience will adore the light-touch approach, but budding Dungeon Masters (especially any drawn to the game because of this Universes Beyond tie-in) would have been well served by a dedicated one-shot guide that eases them into running a game before setting them loose. If you’re looking for an excellent gift for the D&D fan in your life as we head into the holiday season, you’ll be hard-pressed to find a better expansion pick than this. This holds true for the World of Warcraft enjoyer in your life, but consider also offering to run their first game in Azeroth for them. Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.

item.title: REVIEW: Apple iPad mini (OLED, 2026) Review: The Tiniest iPad Is Mightier Than Ever
item.description:
Source: PCMag
With a beefy A20 chip, a gorgeous OLED screen, and a waterproof build, the 2026 Apple iPad mini gets some nice upgrades. But starting at $699, it sits in a curious spot in Apple's lineup. It's smaller, but $250 more expensive than the base iPad, and just $50 less than the highly capable iPad Air. This forces us to ask: Who is this iPad for? Considering its pixel-rich display, top-tier performance, and Apple Pencil support, the iPad mini is ideal if you're a creative who needs a tablet that works as hard as you do. It's an incredible tablet if you prioritize power and portability over price and screen real estate. Ultimately, though, most couch surfers are better off with the standard iPad ($449), our Editors' Choice for affordable tablets and the best iPad for most people, while students should stick to the iPad Air (starting at $749), and professionals should consider the iPad Pro (starting at $1,199). Apple made only the smallest tweaks to the iPad mini's design when compared with its predecessor. It has the same overall appearance: it's a small, rectangular slab with rounded corners, an all-glass front, and an aluminum chassis. The basic look has been this way since 2021. It mirrors the look and feel of the entire iPad lineup, including the base iPad, iPad Air, and iPad Pro. It's a mature look that Apple has no real reason to change or update unless it serves a functional purpose. Perhaps the biggest outward change is the selection of available colors. Where the 2024 iPad mini came in Blue, Purple, Space Gray, and Starlight, the iPad mini (2026) comes only in Midnight (black) or Starlight (light gold). It's a bit disappointing if you're a fan of color. I received the Midnight model for review and appreciate that it is closer to a full black than previous models, which leaned closer to dark gray. The bezels that separate the display from the metal frame are thinner, but Apple hasn't provided exact measurements to say by how much. You can spot the difference only when you place the old and new iPads side by side. Size: A Nip and a Tuck Makes a Difference One of the few differences between the 2026 iPad mini and the previous model is its size and weight. It measures 7.69 by 5.22 by 0.21 inches (HWD) and weighs 0.56 pounds. It retains the same height and width as the 2024 model (7.69 by 5.30 by 0.25 inches, 0.65 pounds), but trims the depth and weight slightly. These tighter measurements may not seem like a lot, but the iPad mini now weighs the same as the iPhone Duo, Apple's folding iPhone. It hardly feels like you're holding anything at all. What about the rest of the iPad lineup? The base iPad only comes in one size (9.79 by 7.07 by 0.28 inches, 1.05 pounds), while the iPad Air and iPad Pro come in two sizes. For the Air, the 11-inch model measures 9.74 by 7.02 by 0.24 inches and weighs 1.02 pounds, and the 13-inch model measures 11.04 by 8.46 by 0.24 inches and weighs 1.36 pounds. The Pro models measure 9.83 by 6.99 by 0.21 inches and weigh 0.98 pounds for the 11-incher, and 11.09 by 8.48 by 0.20 inches and weigh 1.28 pounds for the 13-incher. The iPad mini is by far the smallest and lightest of the lot. What's great about the size is that it fits in small slings, purses, camera bags, and even jacket pockets. Its portability is truly one of its best features. If you're looking for another 8-inch tablet, you'll have to consider an Android slate. There aren't many options, but they include the $529.99 Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 3 (8.21 by 5.10 by 0.31 inches, 0.77 pounds), the $549.99 RedMagic Astra (8.15 by 5.28 by 0.27 inches, 0.82 pounds), or the $229.99 Amazon Alexa Tablet 8 (8.23 by 5.22 by 0.31 inches, 1.01 pounds), which we haven't tested yet. There isn't a comparable Samsung tablet this size. The 2026 iPad mini is the first iPad ever to earn an IP67 rating. This provides good protection against dust and dirt, and against quick submersion in water (up to about 3 feet for up to 30 minutes). This makes it the only iPad you can safely bring to the beach or pool for waterside reading or watching. On the flip side, Apple hasn't called out any special characteristics of the display glass or chassis regarding durability. I reached out to Apple to see whether the mini relies on Ceramic Shield or another specialized glass to protect against scratches and breakage. No other iPad in Apple's lineup meets an IP67 rating. The Legion Tab is rated IP52 (light splashing), and the Astra meets IP54 (rain) and uses Gorilla Glass 3. Apple didn't adjust the location of the buttons and ports. It says the combined power and Touch ID button is thinner, and it does feel narrower than the button on the 2024 iPad mini. The separate volume keys are also on the top edge, but nearer to the other corner. All three buttons have excellent travel and feedback. The USB-C port is centered on the bottom edge. It's a v3.0 port that supports data transfer up to 10Gbps, which is great. You won't find a SIM tray; the cellular version of the iPad mini uses eSIM, same as the 2024 version. You also won't find visible speakers. Apple redesigned the speaker system, and they are no longer built into the side edges. Apple gave the 2026 mini a major display update. It increases in size from 8.3 inches to 8.5 inches, and switches from IPS LCD to Super Retina XDR OLED. It also improves brightness from a max of 500 nits to a peak of 1,200 nits, with the ability to run down to a single nit to save power. It has an incredible 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio and shows deep blacks and rich colors we love to see on OLEDs. The resolution is 2,316 by 1,512 pixels at 324ppi and has P3 wide color, True Tone, an anti-reflective screen coating, and a nano-texture glass option (for $100) that reduces glare. I tested the normal display and have not had a chance to see how well the nano-texture glass works. Some will surely be disappointed that the tablet carries over the 60Hz refresh rate of the older model rather than upgrading to Apple's 120Hz adaptive-rate ProMotion tech. While ProMotion looks fantastic on the iPad Pros, it's worth noting that the iPad mini has a much smaller battery than the Pro models, and 120Hz requires more power to run. Surely, the mini's battery life would take a hit if Apple boosted the refresh rate. Portability often requires some sacrifices, and this is one that's worth making. All the other iPads have larger screens. The base iPad's screen measures 10.9 inches, has a resolution of 2,360 by 1,640 pixels, a density of 264ppi, and a 60Hz refresh rate. It's an LCD with a 500-nit brightness. Both the 11- and 13-inch iPad Airs also have IPS LCD screens. The smaller one has 2,360 by 1,640 pixels at 500 nits, and the larger one has 2,732 by 2,048 pixels at 600 nits. The Pro models have the same Super Retina XDR OLED screen as the mini, but with a faster 120Hz screen. Otherwise, they have the same max brightness (1,600 nits) and nanotexture option. The 11-inch model has a resolution of 2,420 by 1,668 pixels, and the 13-inch model has a resolution of 2,732 by 2,048 pixels, As for other 8-inch tablets, the Legion Tab has an 8.8-inch LCD with a resolution of 2,560 by 1,600 pixels, 900 nits peak brightness, and a max refresh rate of 165Hz. Meanwhile, the Astra has a 9.06-inch OLED display with a resolution of 2,400 by 1,504 pixels, up to 1,600 nits peak brightness, and a max 165Hz refresh rate. The iPad mini's screen may not be as fast as the competition, but it's sharp, bright, and fast enough for most uses. The iPad mini jumps from the A17 Pro in the 2024 model to the same A20 Pro found in the latest iPhone Pros. This is Apple's quickest mobile chip, ensuring you have all the power you need to get your work done. I've written extensively about the A20 Pro, particularly about the novel thermal system Apple used to keep it and the iPhone 18 Pros cool. There are a few things you should know. First, the iPad mini is available in 128GB ($699), 256GB ($799), and 512GB ($999) versions. Add $150 for cellular connectivity. All three come wth 12GB of RAM. I'm a little surprised that Apple is starting at 128GB rather than 256GB, and that there's no 1TB option, though I suppose we can write this all off to the current memory situation. The 128GB and 256GB models have a lower-spec'd version of the chip with a five-core CPU, seven-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, and a 16-core Neural Engine. The 512GB model bumps the CPU to six cores and the Neural Engine to 32 cores (dual 16-core bands). I tested the 512GB model with a faster CPU and more neural grunt. Here are the results of our usual benchmark tests. The Geekbench CPU test took a while to run on the iPad mini. Longer than I've seen it take when compared with other devices I've tested recently. Even so, it scored well, notching 4,030 on the single-core test and 11,303 on the multi-core test. Here's how other devices scored: The only devices that beat the mini are the two M-powered iPads, which isn't a surprise. This test assesses the GPU and its ability to run games. I ran the Wildlife Extreme test, which pushes the GPU for 60 seconds, and it ran 8,308 frames at an average of 49.7 frames per second. It runs more than double the pace of its predecessor. The competition hit these marks: - iPad mini (2024) - 3,109 frames at 18.6fps - iPad Air (2026) - 6,717 frames at 40.2fps - iPad Pro (2025) - 10,929 frames at 65.4fps I'm a little surprised by this result. The M5 iPad Pro is the only tablet to beat the mini, but I expected the M4 iPad Air to be closer. AnTuTu is a rigorous test that runs for more than 10 minutes and assesses how devices perform web tasks such as browsing, rendering photos and videos, and more. The iPad mini scored a total of 3,482,157. Again, the mini scores between the M4 Air and the M5 Pro. This goes to show how powerful the A20 Pro is compared with Apple's M-class chips. In real-world use, the iPad mini flies. Absolutely nothing challenged it, including apps like GarageBand, Lightroom, and, of course, Siri AI. It has all the power you need for most of your workflows. Apple appears to have no interest in pushing iPad battery life past the 10-hour mark. Every iPad released since 2010 has had the same battery life guidance. You can expect about 10 hours of life when browsing at home over Wi-Fi, though you'll lose about an hour if you switch to cellular. Our battery test involves streaming a high-def video from YouTube over Wi-Fi with the screen set to the maximum brightness. The 2024 mini has a 5,034mAh battery, and the 2026 mini has a 4,900mAh battery. The former lasted 7 hours and 23 minutes in our test, while the latter ran for 7 hours and 57 minutes. That's a solid result. What's notable here is the difference in brightness. The 2024 mini's LCD reaches 500 nits at its max, while the 2026 mini's OLED reaches up to 1,600 nits. We didn't measure the actual brightness of the screens in this test, but it's safe to say the 2026 iPad was pushing more nits, which makes its improvement all the more impressive. Other battery results we've recorded: - iPad mini (2024) - 7 hours, 23 minutes When it comes time to recharge, the 2026 iPad mini supports 35W wired charging. Apple says it can reach a 50% charge in 30 minutes. I tested it with a 45W brick, and it hit 50% in 31 minutes and 1005 in 71 minutes. Apple gave the iPad mini the exact same connectivity suite as the iPhone 18 Pro models. That means the C2 modem with 5G and the N1 networking chip with Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread. It's as up to date as you can get for all the radios. Apple supplied me with a 5G-enabled tablet that has active Verizon 5G service, and the speeds I got were impressive. It reached peak speeds of 193Mbps down and 126Mbps up in my neck of NJ, which is limited to C-band. I tested an iPhone 18 Pro Max in the same spots, and it reached peaks of 201Mbps down and 144Mbps up. Wi-Fi speeds reached about the maximum available from my Wi-Fi 6 router at home. The iPad mini hit 850Mbps down and 822Mbps up, while the iPhone notched 891Mbps and 787Mbps, respectively. I had no issues connecting the iPad to accessories such as Bluetooth headphones and smart home products. Apple redesigned the iPad mini's audio system to achieve its IP67 rating. It got rid of the traditional side-firing speakers and outward-facing grilles in favor of invisible tweeters and an Acoustic Display. The tweeters fire through slits that separate the display glass from the aluminum frame. The slits are so narrow you can hardly see them. The woofers sit behind the display glass and fire through them. Apple says this arrangement delivers clearer highs and more direct sound. We don't test tablet speakers for their frequency response, but the iPad mini sounds great. Our test track, The Knife's "Silent Shout," has a punchy bass line that opens the song, and the iPad mini pulsed with the low rhythm before making room for the swelling midrange vocals. Nothing about the iPad's speakers suggested I was listening to anything but regular tweeters and woofers. I switched over to YouTube videos and watched movie trailers, concert footage, and more. The iPad won't fool you into thinking you have a surround sound device in your hands, but the stereo separation is spacious, and the volume is enough to make on-screen explosions feel legit. At its loudest, the iPad mini delivers a consistent 87.7dB, which is quieter than its predecessor, but still loud enough for listening in small spaces, like a bedroom. The most important change you need to know about is that the user-facing camera has moved from the short edge to the long edge. This will make your life easier if you frequently take Zoom or Meet calls during the day, though maybe not if you're a big FaceTime user and accustomed to vertical orientation. The Center Stage camera has a 12MP sensor, an f/2.0 aperture, and records 1080p video at up to 60fps. Extra features include stabilization, broader dynamic range, and time-lapse capture. The screen can act as a Retina Flash if you need it. It's better for video chats than photography. I was not super impressed with the selfies I took. Moreover, the camera doesn't support portrait mode, which is a bummer. I thought the A20 Pro processor would enable this feature. The rear camera is a wide-angle shooter with a 12MP sensor and an f/1.8 aperture. Features include up to 5x digital zoom, Smart HDR 4, and stabilization. If you want to record video, it captures up to 4K60 video and handles extras like slow motion and time-lapse. It takes excellent photos. I brought it outdoors to capture some fall color, and it didn't disappoint. The season's yellows and oranges show through in the samples I shot. They are warm, colorful, and relatively sharp. The tablet supports up to 5x digital zoom, though I suggest you stop at 4x, which is where you'll start to see some grain. It works better than most tablets for taking simple snaps. I was happy with the color, clarity, and tone in the photos I took, which were in line with what I saw that afternoon. The tablet works great for video chats. None of my coworkers caught that I was using it for meetings, rather than the dedicated webcam I normally use. If you're set on recording video clips, the iPad mini runs circles around competing tablets with its clear footage and extra capture modes. It even does well with audio, thanks to its dual-mic capture system. The iPad Pro is still the photo- and video-king of tablets, but the mini is respectably close. Need better photos and videos? Grab an iPhone Pro. The iPad mini ships with iPadOS 27 and updates to version 27.2 when you first boot it. Apple doesn't say how long it will support the mini, but you can expect at least five to six years of system updates. The tablet is powerful enough to run all iPadOS features, including Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. I tested everything. The smaller display is admittedly a little tight for more than two open apps or windows at a time, but you can open, move, and resize multiple app windows to your heart's content. I like that the USB port supports Extended Display, which lets you use an external display to show more apps or windows. That's something the old iPad mini couldn't do. One issue I faced was the menu bar. iPadOS supports a menu bar at the top, as well as a trio of resizing buttons. I found the menu bar was often hard to call up, even in apps that support it. Moreover, the window sizing buttons often get in the way of page-specific actions, like tapping an "x" to close a floating window or web page. This is a small detail I hope Apple and app developers can iron out with updates. Apple Intelligence really works well on the iPad mini. The Apple Photos app is great for editing on the iPad and performing actions like extending the background and reframing with the 3D spatial tool. Apple has pitched the iPad mini as a productivity powerhouse. I gave photo editing in Lightroom a shot and, while it's miles better than editing on an iPhone, the mini's smaller screen isn't as broad a canvas as the screens of the 11- and 13-inch iPads. Most importantly, the software runs flawlessly, with no hangs, crashes, or problems. The iPad mini is compatible with the Apple Pencil USB-C and the Apple Pencil Pro. It supports all the actions those two styli can handle and works well with both. Apple does not make a keyboard accessory for the mini, which is a shame. It could really use a first-party keyboard. Plenty of third-party Bluetooth keyboards are out there, but none are optimized the way an Apple-made one would be. Apple did, however, revise the folio case. It's now made of Apple's Smart Woven material, which is tougher than the leather-like material it used before. The new case is a little thicker than before, more rigid, and more protective.
