item.title: REVIEW: Belkin SoundForm Play ANC Review: Kid-Friendly Headphones That Come Up Short
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The Belkin SoundForm Play ANC ($39.99) are over-ear headphones designed for kids, combining active noise cancelling to create a quiet and focused listening environment while offering an 85dBA volume limit to protect their hearing. The headphones combine tough construction, light waterproofing, and long battery life to be ready for life with a child. Next to our favorite kids' headphones, the $54.99 iClever BTH20, the SoundForm Play ANC costs less but isn't as comfortable to wear and has much worse noise cancellation and harsher audio. Worse, it's easy to disable the volume limiter, something the iClever BTH20 doesn’t allow. With all that in mind, it’s tough to recommend the SoundForm Play ANC—plus there’s always the slightly pricier but equally capable iClever Q950 for older children who want a more adult design. The SoundForm Play ANC headphones are built from a monotone plastic with little distinctive style, which may make them better suited to older children as well. They're available in black, blue, light gray, and pink. The plastic, while cheap-feeling, seems very sturdy. It doesn’t make a peep when being stretched every which way, and it resists that bending quite well. The ear cushion padding is firm, and I found it a bit uncomfortable, though the headband padding is a little softer and supports the headphones’ 7.44-ounce weight well. It's worth noting that they are lighter than the aforementioned iClever models. The headphones have sliders and pivoting yokes to adjust to different head sizes from very small to large. There’s even a slight swivel to adapt to different ear angles, though it’s minor. The firm plastic makes the headphones’ clamping force strong, though, which may bother some kids. The earcups can fold up for storage, but they don’t rotate to sit flat. Belkin also didn’t include a case for portability. The headphones seem sturdy enough not to need one, though. They can also handle a little water with an IPX4 rating. You’ll get fairly rudimentary connectivity from the SoundForm Play ANC. They support a 3.5mm analog connection and don’t require power to run this way. For wireless connections, they use Bluetooth 5.4 and support just the SBC and AAC codecs. They lack Bluetooth Multipoint for connecting to multiple devices simultaneously. The headphones have a second AUX port on the left earcup that can pass audio over to a second headset for sharing via Belkin's RockStar Audio Sharing feature. They can share that audio from wired and Bluetooth sources. It's possible to wirelessly share audio with a second SoundForm Play ANC, but one of the pairs of headphones needs to have no devices with saved pairing data available, so it might not be the most kid-friendly feature to troubleshoot if something goes wrong. The headphones have several on-ear controls. The left earcup has a single ANC control button that cycles through three modes (on, off, and pass-through) with one-second presses. A quick double-tap activates “Focus Boost,” in which each button press cycles through a relaxing background sound. The right earcup has a playback button that can play/pause with a single tap, skip forward with a double tap, and skip backward with a triple tap. There’s also a large volume dial on the right earcup. This dial curiously has hard end stops but is actually a digital dial for controlling volume on the connected device, and for some reason it doesn’t fully mute audio when it’s bottomed out. My phone usually prevents volume increases beyond a certain limit with a warning prompt, but didn’t for these headphones. The headphones support further control if you press the ANC and multifunction button at the same time. By holding them for three seconds, you'll cycle through Belkin Signature Sound, Bass Boost, and Balanced EQ modes, with the first one being the default. Holding these buttons for eight seconds lets you toggle the 85dB volume limiter off and on—which is a big problem, as it means you can't set it and then not have to worry about your kids' hearing. The iClever BTH20 doesn't let you defeat the volume limiter, and it's set to a slightly lower, safer level of 80dB. The power button should be self-explanatory, but I found it a bit bewildering. A two-second press turns the headphones on, but if you hold the button while waiting for them to turn off, they’ll instead enter Bluetooth pairing mode after several seconds. To actually power the headphones off, you must hold the power button for two seconds until you hear a single beep, after which they will seem to do nothing for another two seconds before powering down with a new tone. Some of the settings have voice prompts (with low-quality recordings), so you know what’s what, but others don’t. Ambient sound modes and EQ profiles do, for instance, but entering pairing mode or powering down don’t. The SoundForm Play ANC offers a rated battery life of up to 60 hours, but that drops to 45 hours with noise cancelling enabled. This matches the BTH20 and outperforms the Q950. After about eight hours of use with ANC enabled, the battery had only fallen to 80%, putting it nicely on track to meet the 45-hour rating. The headphones recharge over USB-C with a port on the left earcup. A 10-minute charge should be good for five hours of playback, while the headphones take 100 minutes to charge completely, which really means there’s no fast charging. Belkin includes a USB A-to-C cable, but not a charger. The SoundForm Play ANC doesn’t attenuate much external sound with its passive isolation. It can trim some high-frequency sound, but a lot of noise gets through. That’s where ANC comes in, but the SoundForm Play ANC’s noise cancelling isn’t all that impressive. With an air conditioner running nearby at volumes that are comfortable for extended periods, only some of the lower droning vibration was cancelled out. The sounds from the A/C's fan fall within a higher-frequency range, which is slightly boosted by the ANC mics. The result is that what I heard in the headphones was still about as loud as what I could hear without them. Even with just bass tones coming out of nearby speakers, the headphones don’t prove that impressive at cancelling the sound out. I even caught some incoming sound (a 400Hz sine wave) that caused a high-pitched reverberation in the headphones, sounding like a mosquito in my ear. The headphones also misbehave during sudden changes in pressure. When a nearby door shut in a cafe, it produced a loud, deep pop each time. Opening and closing car doors have the same effect. Wind is another challenge, with the mics clipping from even a light breeze blowing across them, making active noise cancelling fairly useless outdoors. The pass-through mode of the SoundForm Play ANC isn’t great either. It boosts certain higher frequencies, resulting in a somewhat sharp listening experience. Even then, my sense of my surroundings felt incomplete. I couldn’t readily pick up on directionality, and I didn’t get the feeling that my headphones had simply vanished, as I do with quality pass-through. Conversations also prove more difficult. My voice doesn’t come back through the headphones clearly; instead, it sounds overly bassy. This all proves a pretty bad showing for the SoundForm Play ANC, since quality noise cancelling is a good way to help ensure kids won’t want or need to dial the volume up on their headphones to block out distracting external noise. With no audio or sound playing, there’s a constant, noticeable signal noise that’s a little irritating. Sometimes, it’s even perceptible when there’s sound playing. The headphones include several built-in noises called “Focus Boost,” that can play on their own. There’s a rather harsh seashore one, sharp pink noise, and a surprisingly pleasant “Brain Beats” that sounds like I’m in a temple, but this one is sadly marred by that constant signal noise. The SoundForm Play ANC offers tame sound. The Knife’s “Silent Shout” kicks off with punchy bass triplets, but the headphones push them out in mellow fashion. They manage nice, meaty sub-bass quarter notes at least. There’s also a wide soundstage for the panned instruments and phasing effects to sound out. The mids are strong, letting the main elements of the synth melody really bite, though the lower octaves fall into that weak bass realm. Treble is pronounced and somewhat sharp, but it’s also held back by the compression of AAC, which keeps the cymbals and various pads from sounding lifelike and pristine. The headphones continue to hollow out the sound in Kendrick Lamar’s “Loyalty.” The drums wind up lacking, with a kick, rim shots, and cymbals that all fall flat. The high-end makes Rihanna’s voice a bit sibilant and otherwise gives a harshness to the track. To their credit, the headphones do handle sub-bass well. There’s a sub-bass line introduced in the first chorus and played as a frequent refrain, and the headphones play most of the notes nicely, hitting them evenly for a smooth flow. Only the deepest note falls too quiet. The soundstage of the SoundForm Play ANC serves nicely for Bill Callahan’s “Drover,” giving ample space for the instruments to sound out in different spaces. Callahan’s baritone vocals are thinned out by the weak bass, though. And the rhythm guitar, fiddle, and electric guitar all get held back by the muted high-end detail. The emphasis they place on the mids and treble, with too little bass, is a poor match for orchestral music like John Adams’ The Gospel According to the Other Mary. The choir, strings, and brass lack distinction while all sounding harsh. Meanwhile, the low end is almost entirely carved out, leaving only those higher-register instruments crammed together. The mics on the SoundForm Play ANC are typically low-quality, as with many Bluetooth headphones. My voice sounds crackly and a bit hard to make out, and the headphones fail to eliminate background noise effectively. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Belkin SoundForm Play ANC headphones are a letdown overall. They don’t have terrific audio, though they thankfully avoid sounding bad—just a tad harsh at times. That's fine for $39.99. But their promise of noise cancelling is undermined by its poor quality and the issues it creates instead. The more tween-friendly design may have some appeal, but our favorite kids' headphones remain the Editors' Choice iClever BTH20. Meanwhile, iClever’s also-excellent Q950 proves to be a better option for older children. The fact that the SoundForm Play ANC also lets kids turn off its volume limiter, while the iClever headphones won’t, only further keeps us from recommending them. item.title: REVIEW: TP-Link Tapo D260 Doorbell Pro Review: Raising the Resolution Bar
item.description:
Source: PCMag
When I reviewed the TP-Link Tapo D225 ($129.99) last year, I praised its affordable price, sharp 2K image quality, and flexible storage options. With the new Tapo D260 Doorbell Pro, you get even sharper 4K video and the same cloud and local storage options. It includes free intelligent alerts and radar-based motion detection, with aerial footage showing where visitors have traveled while on your property. At $219.99, it’s a bit more affordable than Ring's Battery Doorbell 4K Pro ($249.99), but its cloud subscription plans are more expensive. It’s a solid performer and can be hardwired or run on battery power, but unless 4K video is a must, the Tapo D225 is a better value, so it remains our Editors' Choice for video doorbells. The TP-Link Tapo D260 Doorbell Pro uses a glossy black enclosure with an IP66 weatherproof rating. At 5.7 by 2.5 by 1.4 inches (HWD), it’s one of the larger doorbells I’ve tested. The front of the device holds a camera lens, a doorbell button with an LED ring, motion and light sensors, a pair of infrared LEDS, and a microphone. On the inside, it packs 2.4GHz and 5GHz Wi-Fi radios and a total of 48MB of flash memory. Around the back are two wiring terminals for hardwiring the doorbell; doing so provides unlimited power and 24/7 recording capabilities. Alternatively, you can use the built-in rechargeable battery, which is rated to last up to six months between charges. On the back, you’ll also find a reset button, a microSD card slot, an On/Off button, and an Anti-Theft button. When the anti-theft alarm is enabled on the Tapo app (available for Android and iOS), a 98dB siren will sound if the doorbell is removed. To pause the alarm, press and hold the Anti-Theft button for five seconds. On the bottom edge of the enclosure, you'll find a speaker and a USB-C port for charging the doorbell and powering it with an external power supply if the battery dies. The LED ring shines solid red at startup, slowly blinks red while connecting to Wi-Fi, glows solid amber when connected to Wi-Fi, and glows white when the doorbell button is pressed and when connected to the cloud. The ring uses six white LEDs as a spotlight to enhance color night vision; otherwise, the camera uses the infrared LEDs for black-and-white night vision. The camera captures 4K HDR video at 15fps, offers a wide 180-degree viewing angle for a head-to-toe view of your doorstep, and supports 28.5x digital zoom. It uses radar-based 3D motion detection to reduce false alerts caused by wind, rain, and inconsequential movements. The Aerial View feature, similar to Ring’s Birds’ Eye View, provides an overhead view of motion events with dots that show you where visitors have traveled. Aerial View, local on-board face recognition, and intelligent alerts are included with no extra cost. The TP-Link Tapo D260 Doorbell Pro will record video when the button is pressed or when motion is detected, and store it on a microSD card (up to 512GB, not included), or you can subscribe to a Tapo Care plan to access video in the cloud. TP-Link's most affordable plan includes 30 days of cloud storage for $3.49 monthly, but that tops out at 2K video playback, so it doesn't make sense for this model. The $11.99 per month or $119.99 per year Tapo Care Cloud Advanced plan gives you 180 days of unlimited video storage for an unlimited number of devices, snapshot notifications, smart filters, 24/7 recording, and weekly reports. The $19.99 per month or $199.99 per year Cloud Advanced AI plan includes everything in the Cloud Advanced plan and adds AI facial recognition, intelligent summaries and notifications, video recap, AI video search, AI chat, and custom alerts. By way of comparison, the Ring Solo plan costs $4.99 per month or $49.99 per year and includes 180 days of video history, intelligent alerts (person, package, and vehicle), and extended live view (up to 30 minutes) for a single camera. Ring's Multi plan is $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year and offers the same features as the Solo plan for unlimited cameras, plus an extended warranty. Ring also offers a $19.99 per month or $199.99 per year Pro plan that gives you 24/7 professional monitoring, a feature not offered by TP-Link. The D260 Doorbell Pro uses the same Tapo mobile app as other TP-Link Tapo devices. It appears in its own panel on the My Home screen, alongside any other Tapo devices you have installed. When you tap the panel, it opens a live feed that you can view in full-screen mode by turning your phone sideways. Directly below the video panel are buttons for taking a snapshot, manually recording a video clip, muting the speaker, and placing a voice call to the doorbell. With the voice call feature, you can have a conversation without holding down a button, as you must with two-way talk. Both options offer voice masking to ensure privacy by altering how your voice sounds on the other end. The next group of buttons is for two-way talk, privacy mode (disables streaming and recording), distortion correction (makes wide-angle footage appear more natural), motion tagging (adds a box around moving subjects), quick response (plays a prerecorded message when you can't talk), and subscribing to a Tapo Care plan. Scroll down to access and download recorded video with a timeline of events, configure face recognition, and view a summary of how many recognized and unrecognized faces have been captured. To access the settings screen, tap the gear icon in the upper right corner. Here you can configure storage and recording, video and audio, and Aerial View. Other settings include privacy zones (to block specific areas from view), smart actions (automations), night mode settings, spotlight brightness, motion sensitivity, and network connection. In terms of third-party integrations, the D260 works with Alexa and Google, but it does not support HomeKit or IFTTT applets. The D260 Doorbell Pro comes with a USB-C charging cable, flat and wedged mounting plates, mounting hardware, foam sealing pads, and a user guide. Installing the D260 is easy, but you'll have to download the Tapo app and create an account to get started and charge the battery for at least six to seven hours if you plan to use battery power. Otherwise, just connect the doorbell to your existing wiring using the two terminals on the back. I tapped the plus button in the upper-right corner of the home screen to add a device, then selected Doorbells from the list and chose the Tapo D260. I powered it up, confirmed that the LED had begun flashing red and green, and the doorbell was immediately recognized. I selected my Wi-Fi SSID from the list, entered my password, and waited a few seconds for the doorbell to connect to my network and be added to my Alexa device list. I gave it a name and a location, chose an icon, and then took the doorbell outside and mounted it next to my front door. The D260 delivered outstanding video quality in my tests. Daylight video showed crisp image detail with fully saturated colors, and black-and-white night video was sharp with excellent contrast. Nighttime color quality was good, but the camera needs the white spotlights to capture color video. The camera’s 180-degree field of view provided a full view of my doorstep and most of my front yard. Motion alerts were accurate, and face recognition worked flawlessly. The Aerial View feature worked as intended, showing the footpath of visitors to and from my doorstep. The Anti-Theft siren was loud enough to be heard in every room of my house, and two-way communication was clear and loud. My Alexa voice commands to stream video from the doorbell to an Amazon Echo Show smart display worked perfectly, as did my Alexa routine to have a Tapo L535E light bulb turn red when the doorbell button was pressed. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. At $219.99, the TP-Link Tapo D260 Doorbell Pro isn’t nearly as affordable as its sibling, the Tapo D225 Video Doorbell Camera, but it uses a higher-resolution 4K camera. It also offers local and cloud video storage options, radar motion detection with Aerial View tracking, and facial recognition. It’s a bit more affordable than Ring’s Battery Doorbell 4K Pro, but Ring offers more affordable cloud storage plans with the option of 24/7 monitoring. item.title: REVIEW: SteelSeries Rival Pro review: peak performance with endless playtime
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The SteelSeries Rival Pro offers exceptional performance with plenty of customization options, a lightweight design, and an ingenious ‘infinite’ power supply. It's undoubtedly pricey, but if you want unbeatable gaming features, this is the mouse for you. - +Lightweight with excellent ergonomics - -Matte finish prone to picking up fingerprints Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The SteelSeries Rival Pro feels as if it's really pushing the boundaries of what a gaming mouse can do. Even when I glanced at the specs sheet, I was mightily impressed with the features on offer: interference-free ‘true’ 8K polling, hot-swappable batteries for endless play, and 42,000 DPI sensitivity. But it’s one thing having a good set of specs, and another performing well in practice. So just how good is the SteelSeries Rival Pro? And is it worth its asking price of $179.99 / £169.99 (about AU$250)? Here’s my verdict after hours of testing. First of all, this mouse feels incredibly comfortable to use — in fact, it's up there with some of the best mice as far as ergonomics are concerned. It strikes a happy medium in terms of size, and it fits perfectly in my hand — though it's worth noting that this model is for right-handers only, whereas the ambidextrous form of the SteelSeries Sensei Pro is suited to lefties and righties alike. I use a palm grip style, but the model is also designed to suit those who prefer claw or fingertip as well. I also love how lightweight the Rival Pro is. At 1.9oz / 53g, making sharp movements and adjustments feels supremely swift. The mouse has a lightly textured matte finish that feels, and indeed looks, pretty nice too. Sure, the matte black finish makes it a little prone to picking up fingerprints, but this is more of a nitpick, and this is likely to be less of an issue if you opt for the alternate white colorway. And when it comes to performance, the SteelSeries Rival Pro is equally dazzling. I used it to play Cyberpunk 2077 with the LG UltraGear 25G590B 1000Hz gaming monitor, and was astonished by the sheer responsiveness and precision on offer. Aiming felt incredibly stable and accurate, turning the camera felt super-sharp and reactive, and the high-quality optical switches enabled me to let shots fly snappily and reliably. The mechanical scroll wheel also felt very tactile, with ridges offering great grip. Said optical switches feel great to use for gaming or general productivity, and their mechanical, satisfying sound never felt grating or overzealous to me. Yes, they’re not the quietest switches, so if you prefer a more subdued sound then maybe look elsewhere, but their quality is undeniable — SteelSeries even claims that it tested them for 100 million clicks, so you’ll get plenty of mileage out of this mouse. Feature-wise, this mouse has just about everything you could want. The GG app and web app open up all sorts of customization for binds, sensitivity, polling rate, and power management. I mainly used the web app, and found it incredibly easy to use and make small tweaks here and there. Perhaps the real standout feature, though, is the ‘infinite power system’. You get two batteries with the Rival Pro: one that pops into the mouse itself, and another that you place onto the Ultra Wideband base station. The batteries are hot-swappable, and when your mouse runs flat, you can swiftly substitute in the battery from the base station (which charges while plugged in). As a result, you’ll quite literally never run out of battery — ideal for competitive gamers. While the Rival Pro mouse lacks a USB port for wired play, this infinite power system means you’ll honestly never need it — totally removing any additional weight or awkwardness that comes with a cable connection. With an 8K polling rate, SuperSync — which enables you to independently control tracking and clicking polling rates, and aim tools to boot, it truly feels like the perfect gaming mouse. But are there any real downsides? Well, one thing could prove to put some gamers off: the Rival Pro’s price. At $179.99 / £169.99 (about AU$250), this model is certainly a premium product. Is it worth it? If you want peak performance and essentially endless battery life, then yes. But there are plenty of strong options for less than $100 / £100 out there. All in all, though, the SteelSeries Rival Pro is an innovative, ergonomic gaming mouse with exceptional performance. If you’re looking to take your game up a notch, look no further than this model. SteelSeries Rival Pro review: price & release date - Priced at $179.99 / £169.99 (about AU$250) The SteelSeries Rival Pro was released in October 2026, alongside three other models: the SteelSeries Rival Pro Mini, as well as the SteelSeries Sensei Pro and Sensei Pro Mini. The Rival Pro is priced at $179.99 / £169.99 (about AU$250). That lands it firmly in the premium category, with rivals including the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike and the Razer DeathAdder V4 Pro. Should I buy the SteelSeries Rival Pro? If you’re a pro gamer or an enthusiast, then the features available on the Rival Pro are sure to appeal to you. True 8K polling, 42K DPI sensitivity, and detailed customization options are perfectly suited to competitive play. The Rival Pro has hot-swappable batteries, with one always on charge in the UWB base station. Apart from the five seconds it takes to swap the two batteries, you’ll get unlimited playtime, which is great for gaming tournaments or everyday use. You’re not playing particularly intensive games For a lot of gamers, the features on board are slightly overkill, so if you’re not playing games that require snappy response times, then you’ll probably be better off with a cheaper option. Leading off from that, the Rival Pro is certainly not a model I’d recommend to anyone on a budget. While its performance ensures its still solid value overall, it's hard to look past that steep asking price. SteelSeries Rival Pro review: also consider We were blown away by this Logitech mouse when we tested it earlier this year. Its ultra-low click and sensor latency, brilliant switches, and impressive build quality are hard to beat — even if it's pretty pricey. Read our full Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike review. The Razer DeathAdder V4 Pro is a top-tier gaming mouse, boasting flawless performance, a great optical scroll wheel, and beautiful ergonomics. It's similarly priced to this SteelSeries rival, but we’ve seen it pop up on sale from time to time. Read our full Razer DeathAdder V4 Pro review. - Used for gaming and general productivity - Made use of all features in the GG web app I spent many hours testing the SteelSeries Rival Pro, during which time I used it for gaming and general productivity. When gaming, I paired the mouse with the LG UltraGear 25G590B 1000Hz gaming monitor to get the best performance possible. I made sure to play a range of games, but mainly tested the mouse with the PC version of Cyberpunk 2077. On top of this, I made sure to try out all of the mouse’s features and customization options via the GG web app. More generally, I’ve spent years testing gadgets here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve reviewed everything from premium Dolby Atmos soundbars to gaming software, and have tested a number of mice, including the recently released Logitech Mobi Fold.

item.title: SALES: This $60 car jump starter doubles as a power bank and flashlight
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
You do not want to be stuck far from home with a dead car battery and no way to jump start it. A portable jumper is essential to keep as a backup in your car, allowing you to jump a dead car without relying on another vehicle and without needing extra jumper cables. The Povasee Jump Starter Power Bank is current $59.97 at Amazon, which is a big 40% discount off its original $99.99 and close to its all-time lowest price. That’s a reasonable price to pay for peace of mind, knowing you’ll have a savior in your trunk in times of need. What the Povasee Jump Starter Power Bank offers The Povasee Jump Starter Power Bank is a 3-in-1 gadget: not only a portable jumper for emergencies, but also a power bank that can charge your devices and an LED flashlight with multiple modes. With a battery capacity of 74 Wh and a peak current of 5,000 amps, it works with 12V vehicles with up to 10L gas engines or 8L diesel engines. At full charge, it can provide approximately 60 jump-starts. That battery power can also be used to charge devices via two USB-A ports, compatible with phones, tablets, headphones, smartwatches, and more. It comes with a pair of plug-in jumper cables equipped with 10 protective features, including protections against short circuits, overcharging, overheating, and reverse polarity. It’s designed to work in extreme temperatures, too, ranging from -4°F to 140°F. The package also includes a USB-C charging cable. The built-in LED flashlight has three modes of operation: a solid light, a flashing strobe light, and an SOS pattern for emergencies. It comes in handy whether you just need extra light while camping or your car won’t jump at night and you’re stranded on the side of the road. Measuring 6.7 x 3.3 x 1.7 inches and weighing 2.2 pounds, it’s pretty compact—certainly enough to fit in your trunk or backseat. item.title: SALES: The TechCrunch Founder Summit agenda is only half the reason to be in Boston on November 4

item.title: SALES: Best gaming laptops 2026: 4 top options for portable performance
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Gaming laptops have a lot more variety than most people think. That’s why it’s important to know a thing or two about them when shopping for one. There are some machines that deliver raw performance over anything else, and others that prioritize color-accurate displays. But the real test is how they actually hold up when gaming. And that’s where we come in! At PCWorld, we’ve put every laptop on this list through hands-on testing. And we didn’t just stop at the specifications, either! We looked at everything, including keyboard feel, port placement, performance consistency, and display quality. Why you should trust PCWorld for laptop reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld prides itself on laptop experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review more than 70 laptops every year. All of the picks below have been personally tested and vetted by our experts, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. We’re also committed to reviewing PC laptops at every price point to help you find a machine that matches your budget. Alienware 16X Aurora – Best gaming laptop overall - You can get better gaming performance with a faster GPU (of course) Who should buy the Alienware 16X Aurora? If you want a high-end gaming laptop that punches well above its price point, the Alienware 16X Aurora is the one to spring for. It’s fast, powerful, and surprisingly good value for what you’re getting. The Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX CPU is an absolute beast for gaming (or productivity!), and the RTX 5070 graphics handles modern titles just fine at high settings, even at higher resolutions. Whether you’re jumping straight into AAA games or streaming your favorite titles, this laptop will definitely keep up. The 16-inch 2560×1600 IPS display is bright, colorful, and buttery-smooth thanks to its 240Hz refresh rate. It’s great for competitive gaming or fast-paced action games. You also get a full-sized keyboard, a responsive trackpad, and a crisp 1080p webcam with Windows Hello face login. The build is solid, too. It feels premium and the design doesn’t lean very much into the flashy gamer aesthetic. Alienware 16X Aurora: Further considerations The Alienware 16X Aurora isn’t the lightest laptop in the room at 5.86 pounds and that’s okay. The aluminum and plastic construction keep it premium-feeling, though it does pick up fingerprints more than we’d like. The keyboard and trackpad also aren’t the best. The RTX 5070 GPU isn’t top of the line, but it offers plenty of oomph for high-end gaming at 1440p. If it’s a fancy OLED display and an all-metal build you’re after, you’ll definitely pay significantly more for those features. Finally, battery life is about average for a gaming laptop (we eked out seven hours on a single charge), but you’ll probably be plugged in anyway for those intense matches. Acer Nitro V 16 – Best gaming laptop under $1,000 - Large touchpad compared to alternatives - Good battery life for a budget gaming laptop - Terrible audio quality from built-in speakers - Wireless connectivity stuck on the Wi-Fi 6 standards - Slightly more expensive laptops offer better value Who should buy the Acer Nitro V 16? If you’re a gamer on a budget who wants modern RTX 50-series performance, you can’t get much better than the Acer Nitro V 16 AI. The RTX 5050 GPU handles most 1080p games smoothly, hitting high frame rates in titles like Rise of the Tomb Raider and even running more intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077 at playable settings. This laptop also offers surprisingly good battery life. You can get anywhere from eight to 12 hours on a single charge depending on usage. Plus, the 16-inch 1200p display at 180Hz is slightly better and smoother than the standard 15.6-inch 1080p screens on similar budget laptops. There are some trade-offs to keep in mind. First, the Ryzen 5 240 CPU is entry-level, so CPU-heavy tasks like video editing or streaming may feel sluggish if you’re pushing the machine pretty hard. Storage and RAM are also limited to 512GB and 16GB. That’s fine for gaming, but it could require updates over time. Speakers and webcam are also basic, and Wi-Fi isn’t cutting-edge. Razer Blade 14 (2025) – Most portable gaming laptop - Bulkier gaming laptops will perform better Who should buy the Razer Blade 14 (2025)? Looking for a gaming laptop that won’t kill your back? The Razer Blade 14 (2025) is only 3.59 pounds, which is crazy light for a beast like this. It’s packing an AMD Ryzen AI 9 365 CPU and an RTX 5070 GPU, so it can easily handle modern games on High or Ultra settings. The 14-inch 2880×1800 120Hz OLED screen is a delight to behold and, somehow, the laptop itself manages to stay cool and quiet even when it’s under load. Oh, and that matte-black finish? Pretty slick. Razer Blade 14 (2025) : Further considerations It’s not cheap or super flashy, but it hits the sweet spot for power and portability. Battery life is pretty good for a gaming laptop (just over 11 hours!), but don’t expect to game unplugged all day. The keyboard and touchpad are fine, speakers could be better. Still, if you want a capable gaming rig that you can carry with ease, this one’s worth it. Alienware Area-51 – Best high-end gaming laptop - Excellent optional mechanical keyboard - Lots of physical connectivity including Thunderbolt 5 Who should buy the Alienware Area-51? If you want a super-powerful gaming laptop, the Alienware Area-51 fits the bill. It’s made for enthusiasts who don’t want to be tethered to a gaming tower. Inside it’s got an Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX processor and RTX 5080 graphics, so it’s well-equipped to handle demanding games at high settings. Visuals look gorgeous, too. The 16-inch 2560×1600 OLED display delivers deep blacks and vibrant colors. The 240Hz refresh rate (plus G-Sync support!) also makes it a good fit for fast-paced gaming. Alienware Area-51: Further considerations The Alienware Area-51 is designed to be a desktop replacement, a role it excels in. The real trade-offs here are portability and price. It’s a beastly thing at more than 7 pounds. The high-end hardware also comes at a premium price. This configuration, for example, costs well over $4,000. We’ve also tested a few other gaming laptops that impressed us, even though they didn’t make the final cut in the end. The Maingear Super 16 is an absolute beast of a laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX, an RTX 5070 Ti, 32GB of RAM, a 2TB SSD, and a 16‑inch 2560×1600 300 Hz display, but it’s expensive–you’ll spend well over $2,000. The Acer Predator Helios Neo 14 AI, on the other hand, is a more compact machine. It’s got an Intel Core Ultra 9 285H processor, an RTX 5070, and a 14.5-inch 2880×1800 120Hz OLED panel, and it’s on sale for just $1,499.99 at Amazon right now. at the time of this writing. And then we’ve got the Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo, which is the unicorn of the gaming laptop world. It’s got two 16-inch OLED 2880×1800 displays that you can position either horizontally or vertically. The PCWorld team puts each and every Windows laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, undergo a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops. Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo, and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also really into the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed, from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound, Allen. To find the best gaming laptop for your needs, pay close attention to the following features. What’s the best screen for a gaming laptop? When you buy a gaming laptop, one of the most important decisions you’ll need to make regards the screen. After all, what you get on day one is what you’re stuck with until you junk the device. You could run an external monitor, but then what’s the point of a laptop? Look for an IPS or OLED display, though gaming laptops under $1,000 sometimes feature a TN panel. You can get by with a 60Hz display if you mostly play single-player games, but thankfully, most gaming laptops these days opt for faster 120Hz+ panels instead. What’s the best screen size for a gaming laptop? The size of the screen dictates the size of the laptop itself, and thus weight. Think long and hard about whether you’re willing to take the weight penalty in exchange for the screen real estate. What’s the best screen resolution for a gaming laptop? The buzzword today is “4K.” That high resolution delivers sharper photo viewing and more space for video editing, but that doesn’t mean it’s for everyone. Anything not using the panel’s native resolution of 3840×2180, such as games running at lower-than-4K resolution, won’t look quite as sharp unless you exponentially increase the graphics power of the laptop. If you’re running at 1920×1080 resolution because your GPU can’t hit 60fps at 4K, that feature is moot. For many gamers, 1920×1080 (1080p) or 2560×1440 (1440p) is more optimal. IPS vs. TN vs. OLED: What’s the difference? The panel technology is a key feature. IPS (in-plane switching) generally produces much greater color accuracy and superior off-axis viewing, but tends to lag in response times, which can lead to blurring. TN (twisted nematic) panels can offer far higher refresh rates and usually better response times than IPS, but can look washed out or just blah. A middle-ground technology that’s appearing more often is VA (vertical alignment). VA is sometimes alternately referred to as “wide viewing angle” technology. (Many assume this spec to be IPS, but it’s not). In our experience, we’ve found VA panels to run the gamut from being worthy competitors to IPS to being worse than the better TN panels. The wildcard in all this is OLED. Unlike IPS, TN, and VA, OLED panels don’t rely on edge- or backlighting where “black” is produced by a shutter-like mechanism that blocks light from coming through. Instead, each pixel generates its own light. To produce black, it just switches off the light. This amounts to truly stunning contrast ratios and vibrant colors. OLEDs also boast fantastic response times. The negatives include smaller screen sizes (we haven’t seen anything larger than 15.6 inches yet), higher cost, and lack of support for variable refresh rate. OLED panels can also use more power than conventional methods if the image is on a white background. Should a gaming laptop have G-Sync or FreeSync support? Okay, we called this section G-Sync and FreeSync, but the reality is, when it comes to beefy gaming laptops, it’s a GeForce GPU world. And that means it’s a G-Sync world. In a nutshell, Nvidia and AMD’s respective variable-refresh-rate technologies help synchronize the monitor and the GPU to greatly reduce screen tearing. Variable refresh rates can make gaming at 40fps far smoother to your eyes than a screen without it. The first variable-refresh-rate panels for laptops maxed out at 75Hz, only marginally better than the standard 60Hz. More recently, we’ve begun to see laptop panels that can push 120Hz, 144Hz, and even 240Hz. This generally means smoother and sharper gaming to your eyes. It even helps smooth out everyday tasks such as scrolling a browser page or Word document. One last very important note: G-Sync screens have to be connected directly to the laptop’s discrete GPU, which means a large hit on battery life. In most laptops without G-Sync, the Intel integrated graphics is connected directly to the screen, so the GPU can be turned off when not being used. So while G-Sync is beautiful to behold, the cost in battery life is huge. What should you look for in a gaming laptop keyboard and trackpad? A new trend in gaming laptops is the offset trackpad, which is more conducive to gaming than a dead-center trackpad. The concept is sound, but anyone who actually cares about PC gaming will just plug in a mouse. The worst thing about that offset trackpad is when you try to use it for non-gaming purposes. As far as keyboards go, the most important gaming feature is n-key rollover. This means the keyboard physically scans each key separately. If you wanted to, you could press 20 keys simultaneously and they’d all register, as each is independently wired. That probably sounds excessive, but keyboards that lack this feature can suffer missed keystrokes, which both ruins gameplay and hurts in everyday tasks. Other keyboard considerations include LED backlighting (which adds ambiance but does nothing for gameplay) and mechanical keys vs. membrane. Mechanical keys are excellent, but are available on only a handful of laptops that usually weigh a ton. We have seen a few designs with low-profile mechanical keyboards, but even we admit they can be an acquired taste. What kind of storage is best for a gaming laptop? Having your games load from an SSD instead of a hard drive significantly cuts down on load times. But beyond that, we haven’t found it to matter that much whether it’s a super-fast NVMe PCIe drive or a slower SATA SSD. What does matter more today is the size of the SSD rather than the interface it uses. With games now topping 50GB and some touching 100GBs, a once-spacious 256GB SSD will feel too small with just four games installed. So when spec’ing out that gaming laptop, be mindful of just how much total storage you have. If you go for a laptop with a small SSD and large hard drive combo, expect to install your games to the hard drive. If the laptop will have an SSD only, choose an absolute minimum of 512GB, with 1TB preferred. How much RAM do you need in a gaming laptop? When laptop makers spec out gaming laptops, one of the levers they use to try to convince you to buy their product is upping the amount of RAM. It’s not hard to find gaming laptops with “upgraded” configurations that go from 16GB of RAM to 32GB. While having an adequate amount of RAM is important for gaming, today’s games typically top out at 16GB of RAM, and sometimes can run fine with just 8GB of RAM. Most people should invest in a gaming laptop with 16GB of memory if possible, and it makes sense to opt for 32GB if you plan on holding onto your gaming laptop for a long time. Modern games are only getting more memory-hungry. Should a gaming laptop have dual-channel or single-channel RAM? Besides the amount of memory, a couple of other important, but not critical, questions to ask is what clock speed and what mode. Modern CPUs let you run RAM in sets to increase the memory bandwidth. More memory bandwidth immediately helps laptops that are running integrated graphics, but the conventional wisdom has long been that discrete GPUs in laptops don’t benefit as much because they have their own dedicated, much faster GDDR5 RAM to use. That’s typically the case, but the performance of today’s GPUs and CPUs can make this conventional wisdom wrong. Gaming performance is often about a balance between the CPU and the GPU, and how graphically intensive a game is. With games that are graphically intensive, the GPU is the primary bottleneck on performance. Play a game that isn’t graphically intense, though, and the CPU can rapidly become the bottleneck on performance. With the power of today’s GPUs, a lot of games, especially at a sedate resolution of 1920×1080, have shifted more performance to the CPU. The reason we’re talking about this now is if you rob the CPU of memory bandwidth, even a decently fast one, you can take a sizable hit in gaming performance. The basic lesson is you should opt for dual-channel memory bandwidth configurations when possible. On a laptop spec sheet, you typically would see this expressed as “dual-channel” or “2 x 8” to indicate that two 8GB memory modules were used in a laptop. Some laptop makers will express memory in clock speed, so you’ll see “DDR4/2,133 or DDR4/2,400.” While a higher memory clock does increase memory bandwidth, the impact isn’t quite as great as going from dual-channel to single-channel mode. How many CPU cores do you really need in a gaming laptop? For most people on a budget, a 4-core CPU with Hyper-Threading will function just fine in most games, especially when combined with a lower-cost and lower performance GPU. Still, if you have the extra cash, a 6-core CPU with Hyper-Threading is likely the sweet spot for today and tomorrow. If you plan to stream your gaming live or edit it, investing in a 6-core is recommended. Intel and AMD’s top-end 8-plus-core CPUs will deliver the greatest benefit to those who might do other graphics-intensive tasks, such as 3D animation or video editing. If you also plan to record and stream video, the 8-core will offer a performance benefit there, too. If you’re thinking, great, let me buy a 4-core Core i5 or Ryzen 5 CPU with a luxury laptop to save money, you usually can’t, because PC makers typically only offer budget CPUs with other budget parts. Why? Well, most budget shoppers can’t afford any luxury items, and most PC makers like to add in the extras to increase the profit. What GPU is best for a gaming laptop? The single most important piece of hardware in a gaming laptop is undoubtedly the GPU. For AMD fans, the situation is as sad as it is in CPUs: It’s an Nvidia GeForce world. As with CPUs though, the good news is that the dominating products are top-notch. The hardest part will be deciding just how much GPU you need. Our general guidance is to buy as fast a GPU as you can afford and are willing to heft. Generally, the faster the GPU (or GPUs), the larger and heavier the laptop. If you’re talking about playing on a higher-resolution panel of 2560×1440 at high-refresh rates, then keep increasing the amount of money spent on the GPU. What kind of battery life should a gaming laptop have? The last topic we’ll cover is battery life. The best way to understand battery life on a gaming laptop is to accept that it’ll be horrible for all things gaming. The minute you crank up a GPU on a gaming laptop to play a game, you’re basically limiting yourself to an hour or an hour and a half of battery runtime. Period. And in some cases, far less than that. The only reason to consider battery life on a gaming laptop is if you want to use your laptop unplugged for non-gaming purposes. In that respect, you’ll find a lot of variance, with some offering decent battery life, albeit with a trade-off in gaming performance. What is the best gaming laptop? The Alienware 16X Aurora is PCWorld’s top gaming laptop, delivering high-end performance without the ridiculously high price tag. What is the best cheap gaming laptop? The Acer Nitro V 16 AI is PCWorld’s top budget gaming laptop. It offers good gaming performance and a spacious 16-inch, 1200p display for a low price. When is the best time to buy a gaming laptop? The best time to pick up a gaming laptop is during Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or back-to-school season. Those deals will save you a lot of cash. Should you get a gaming laptop or a PC? It really depends on your lifestyle. If you’re someone that’s always on-the-go, a gaming laptop is a good fit. But if you’re okay with staying in one spot and want more power or upgrade options, a PC is a better choice. What’s the difference between a gaming laptop and a regular laptop? A gaming laptop is made for handling games, so it has beefed-up graphics and better cooling. A regular laptop, on the other hand, is designed for everyday stuff like browsing or working on documents and operating unplugged for extended periods of time.

item.title: SALES: Christmas markets UK 2026: 16 best to visit this festive season
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
For the most magical Christmas markets, UK cities and small English villages are my favourite places to explore during the festive period. I know countries like Germany and Austria are famous for their incredible Christmas festivities, but from Scotland to Devon, there is something special to do in every corner of the country. There is no need to fly anywhere in December, as the UK is home to some of the world's most magical Christmas markets. Around early November, something inexplicably wondrous begins to happen – somewhere, in between all the gripes and groans about darker mornings, colder evenings and blustery days, little flickers of joy begin to crack through the frost. Fairy lights appear, wrapped around trees or dangling from ceilings; shop fronts suddenly have a Christmassy sheen thanks to their festive window displays; scents of festive spices float out of cafés and restaurants. And, best of all, sprawling squares and cobbled alleys get filled with wooden stalls and trestle tables laden with sparkling trinkets, giant pots of hot toddy and mulled wine, and cutesy stocking fillers. All of a sudden, before you know it, Christmas is upon us – and you forget all about those winter grumbles and embrace the season in all its twinkling glory. From traditional German-style markets serving bratwurst and mulled wine to independent stalls selling handmade gifts, the best Christmas markets in the UK are worth planning a festive weekend around. Which city has the best Christmas market in the UK? Manchester is one of the best cities in the UK for Christmas markets, with more than 210 stalls spread across 10 locations in the city centre in 2026. Visitors can browse everything from handcrafted gifts and festive decorations to seasonal food, mulled wine and sweet treats. There's also an ice skating rink in Cathedral Gardens, a Ferris wheel in Albert Square and plenty of festive entertainment. Other favourites include Bath, with its picturesque Georgian streets, Edinburgh, where the Christmas market takes place beneath the city's historic skyline, and Birmingham's Frankfurt Christmas Market, known for its traditional German atmosphere. What is the most Christmassy town in the UK? York is certainly one of the most Christmassy places in the UK, thanks to its medieval streets, historic architecture and traditional festive celebrations. Every winter, the city transforms into a festive destination, with twinkling lights, market stalls selling gifts and seasonal treats, and plenty of cosy pubs to escape the cold. York Christmas Market, also known as St Nicholas Fair, returns from 12 November to 21 December 2026, although the market will be closed on Tuesdays this year. Which is the biggest Christmas market in the UK? Manchester Christmas Markets is widely considered one of the biggest in the UK, with more than 210 stalls spread across 10 locations in the city centre for 2026. Birmingham's Frankfurt Christmas Market, meanwhile, is recognised as the largest authentic German Christmas market outside Germany and Austria, with traditional wooden stalls selling everything from pretzels and bratwurst to festive gifts and decorations. For those looking for a larger festive experience beyond traditional market stalls, London's Hyde Park Winter Wonderland combines Christmas shopping with fairground rides, a giant Ferris wheel, an ice skating rink and live entertainment. Here are some more of our Christmas round-ups to enjoy: What to know before you visit a UK Christmas market Word to the wise: Christmas markets in the UK can be as chaotic as they are fun. Some of these markets are rather vast, and giddy visitors tend to crowd around the most popular areas and prettiest stalls, so be prepared. Remember that the majority of these markets are outdoors, so wrap up warm with cosy scarves, woollen gloves and toasty coats. item.title: SALES: 18 best restaurants in Budapest right now for a tasty trip
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Whenever anyone comes to visit Budapest, the requests immediately begin pouring into me. They want massive portions of stuffed cabbage and gulyás – in Hungary, it’s a soup, not a stew – and they want to savour them in a family-owned restaurant that’s lasted for generations and brimming with personality. If the trip coincides with the must-see crammed Christmas markets or summer sojourns to Lake Balaton, then they also want lángos, addictive orbs of fried dough more commonly served on the street than in a restaurant. Hungarian cooking is heavy but it’s soulful and signifies memory. There are standbys I recommend over and over again for this type of cuisine – Rosenstein, Café Kör, Pozsonyi Kisvendéglő, and Gettó Gulyás among them, for they all are eye-opening portals into Hungarian culture. But alongside this conventional palate, it’s the breadth of global flavours that I find particularly exciting. The queues at #1 Birria Taco Bar are constant. Wonton dumplings, shaped by hand, have the crowds ordering from Zhu and Co. Eating inside a Japanese grocery store, as one does at Kicsi Japán, is exhilarating. Equally electrifying is the increasing predilection for natural wines sipped alongside small, ingenious plates. Budapest is a city that deftly melds tradition and modernity, but right now there’s something particularly engaging about the contemporary side of the culinary scene. It fosters laughter and conversation in good-looking places that a predictable three-course meal simply can’t. Here’s where to soak up that stirring atmosphere. Best for: natural wines fortified by imaginative small plates It's easy to lose track of time at Cabrio. The banquette that snakes around the large windows, the loungey music, and the perfect warm lighting are all invitations to stay for a while, and that's exactly what Benjamin Tenner, Jónás Togay, and Bence Szilágyi want guests to do at their modern European bistro, seemingly plucked from the 11th arrondissement of Paris. Natural wines, increasingly popular in Budapest, are showcased here (try Szilágyi's own label, Barnag, made in the Balaton uplands), best complemented by thrilling small plates like burnt celeriac carpaccio dressed in a walnut vinaigrette, braised shredded beef cheek atop brioche, and a hefty chocolate crème brûlée from chef Tomi Albrecht of MÓR24. Address: Vitkovics Mihály u. 3-5, Budapest 1052 Dish to order: spicy beef plonked into a two-flavour broth base of spicy and Thai Budapest has a thriving Chinese community, and it's centred in far-flung District X. That's where locals venture to when they crave the fiery Sichuan dishes at Spicy Fish and HeHe Chinese Restaurant, or the excellent hotpot on offer at In Town. In the middle of Chinese-style tables planted underneath dangling lanterns (book a private nook in advance), broths – go for the lime-scented Thai and spicy versions – are ladled into enormous pots. Then, carts roll up with thinly sliced beef (the spicy one is especially delightful), lotus root disks, tangled strands of potato, and all manner of tofu. Thrust them into the bubbling liquids, chat as they cook before invigorating them in sesame-chilli sauces, and pause between rounds with endless cups of chrysanthemum tea. Best for: confections that taste as divine as they look Dropping by historic Café Gerbeaud should be obligatory, for who wants to miss out on a slice of its eponymous chocolate glazed cake with ground walnuts and apricot jam in a splendorous late 19th-century room? But Egy csipet torta, minutes from the Hungarian Parliament Building, reimagines the old-school cukrászda(confectionery) with pretty desserts served in a fresh, muted setting. Along with enticing slabs of carrot cake, Sacher torte, and dacquoise-layered Esterházy the founders, pastry chef Alexandra Horváth and Levente Biró, ensure the glass display case is updated with seasonal specialities fusing unexpected elements like sweet and sour pear with spicy chai cremeux. A whimsical array of bundt pans on the wall hints that the fudgy kuglóf is a modest, unsuspecting hit. Best for: an innovative spin on fine dining Bi-level Fiktív is reinterpreting fine dining. Unlike some of its fussier brethren, it has a laid-back air with artworks of farm animals gracing the grey walls, a living room-style gallery space upstairs, and unconventional beverage pairings running the gamut from Calvados to fermented non-alcoholic cocktails to the homemade tea capping off meals. The à la carte and shockingly affordable eight- and 10-course tasting menus, kicked off with gratis glasses of sparkling wine and rustic bread begging to be slathered with shallot-onion laden butter, come courtesy of chef Márton Tatai. Previously of the iconic Onyx restaurant, he has a flair for melding surprising ingredients like cabbage, peanut, buttermilk, and fig leaf oil, as well as rooster, kohlrabi, and hake, an avant-garde twist on a humble Hungarian favourite. Best for: cosy, out-of-the-way, upgraded Hungarian feasts Light, airy Szaletly is in Zugló, a residential neighbourhood not far from City Park, and executive chef Dániel Bernát has made frequent diners of many of the residents nearby. The mismatched furniture gives it the vibe of dining at a friend's house, and the seasonal dishes heighten Hungarian flavours by mingling them with ingredients like daikon radish relish and Jerusalem artichoke. Begin with the beef tartare, lifted with black garlic mayonnaise and fermented kohlrabi, then dive into veal Cordon Bleu buoyed by cheese from the Lake Balaton area before ending with the egg liqueur-baked poppy seed bread pudding. There are also reasonably priced tasting menus, including a vegetarian one starring the restaurant’s signature layered potatoes sans the Mangalica sausage from Debrecen. Best for: a vibrant vegetarian breakfast Dish to order: poached eggs with garlic yoghurt Tapping into her Turkish roots, Merve Ilgim Deprem first established Garden Café in the back of a boutique selling indie clothing and jewellery. Now, the retail aspect is gone and all eyes are on her relaxed vegetarian hangout. Savour breakfasts of cilbir, poached eggs with garlic yoghurt, chilli, brown butter, dill, and sourdough bread, or spicy potato gözleme, finished off with a pistachio cream-baklava pancake for dessert. Come evening, the Garden morphs into Pebbles, a natural wine bar and kitchen that finds inspiration in the Aegean coast. Delicious bakeries abound in Budapest. Arán, Artizan, Lui, and Läget, are responsible for some of the city's finest breads and pastries, but sometimes the vast assortments can be overwhelming to navigate. Déryné Kenyer's tightly edited lineup is enchanting because it seems foolish to leave without trying almost everything. Order the csiga, the flaky snail-shaped pistachio pastry, the shiny, miniature scone-like potato pogacsa, and the savoury parmesan pretzel, while locals pop in for loaves of sourdough. Many of them are likely loyalists of Déryné, the bistro next door, kitted out with a black and white floor and plants that have long captivated the well-heeled Buda set. Dish to order: roasted pork tenderloin "Brassói" style Szabina Szulló and Tamás Széll woo guests night after night at their two Michelin-starred restaurant, Stand, in District VI, but those who would rather not splurge on fine dining can head over the Chain Bridge to Stand25, their more casual outpost. Here, innovative takes on European classics like French onion soup or Chicken Kiev are plated up in a startlingly bright neon kitchen. But the main appeal is the jazzed-up Hungarian dishes. The rich gulyás is a beauty, as is the "Brassói"-style pork tenderloin with its mélange of roasted potatoes and cucumbers, and the pancakes bursting with Piedmont chocolate-hazelnut cream. Best for: a quick Hungarian lunch in a nostalgic atmosphere Dish to order: breaded chicken breast and mashed potatoes Sadness ensued when the personable Ilona Sebestyénné Földes, better known as Cica Néni among her mobs of regular diners, announced she was shutting down Róma Ételbár, a Buda institution. Luckily, one of those fans, Dániel Andrusch, swooped in to save it. First opened in 1990, Róma Ételbár is one of the city's few remaining lunch-only étkezdes. There's crispy schnitzel-style chicken served over mounds of mashed potatoes, duck leg with steamed purple cabbage, and plump túrógombóc, cottage cheese dumplings draped under sour cream. With its vintage radio, checkered tablecloths, and constellation of photographs on the walls, Róma Ételbár conjures the soothing aura of dining in a relative’s home. Fans of the tapas at Padron and Arquitecto Pitpit in District VIII immediately swooned for Monokini Kantin, the group’s latest project, when it threw open its doors. Led by chef Ádám Garai, who has a fine dining background, the restaurant brightens Buda’s District II with its mix of Spanish and Japanese flavours. Crispy caper-studded smoked potato salad, mushroom gyoza in brown butter-peanut sauce, and daily-changing ramen all share the table in this casual, light-filled space adorned with black-and-white artworks and minimalist benches and stools. Address: Budapest, Varsányi Irén u. 33, 1027 Best for: old-world Hungarian vibes with a fresh attitude For more than six decades, Kádár Étkezde held court on Klauzal tér in District VII, and when it closed in 2020, the sense of loss was profound. But Hungarian entrepreneur Károly Gerendai, best known as the founder of the music festival Sziget, revived the lunchtime go-to in 2025, and locals are overjoyed. Inside the bigger, refurbished restaurant, the old-fashioned touches – the panelling, the heaps of memorabilia – gratefully remain in place. Gorging on stuffed cabbage and breaded pork cutlets atop ribbons of spaghetti, the ambience transports diners to a bygone time. Dish to order: spicy Sichuan spinach at 101 Bistro Time Out Markets enliven cities like Lisbon, Osaka, and Vancouver. The Budapest outpost, housed in a 1926 department store in a busy stretch of District VIII, has beautiful, historic bones. Joining the roster of such local favourites as 101 Bistro, Pingrumba, and Szaletly is Fúzió by Textúra & Borkonyha, chef Ákos Sárközi’s love letter to Hungary starring roast pork brioche ramped up with thyme sauce. Beyond Budapest dishes, taste pizza from Anyukám Mondta, a chic restaurant in northern Hungary, or fisherman’s soup from Lake Balaton hotspot Casa Christa. Then, sample the country’s diverse wine regions with a tasting at the Wines of Hungary bar. Website: timeout.com/time-out-market-budapest Best for: Delicious food from a young, brazen chef rounded out with DJ vibes. Horváth Mihály tér, in Budapest’s gritty District VIII, is one of the city’s biggest surprises. Just steps away from St. Joseph Church, a graceful Baroque stunner, there’s Kozmo Hotel & Suites, a former telecommunications center rife with Art Nouveau details, and Orma, the plant-based bakery that originated in Pécs, in southern Hungary. KOHO, the bi-level restaurant from Mark Blazek and Ágnes Nagyistók fits right in. Its raw, Brutalist sheen first makes a striking impression, but perching at the chef’s counter reveals a great culinary depth, too. József Tóth is only in his early 20s, but he’s well-traveled and possesses an old soul, a remarkable combination that manifests in a cooking philosophy that bridges Hungarian ingredients with French techniques and Japanese minimalism. Consider Tóth’s trout, a menu mainstay currently heightened by plum, daikon, and coffee ponzu, or the steak, arguably Budapest’s best, incorporating a Kyoto carrot puree and quince salsa. While it’s tempting to stay upstairs and watch the kitchen in action, the dark, moody subterranean space can’t be missed. Bring back the art of the progressive dinner by tucking into the deconstructed Black Forest cake downstairs in the company of cookbooks revered by the contemplative Tóth. Address: 14 Horváth Mihály tér, Budapest 1082 Best for: special-occasion dining that conjures Old-World Hungary Small, dynamic restaurants are deservedly garnering all the accolades in Budapest right now. But it doesn’t mean that stalwarts like Babel should be forgotten. The charismatic entrepreneur Hubert Hlatky-Schlichter first introduced Budapest gourmands to Babel in 2008. Later, it moved to its current location in an old high school (Hlatky-Schlichter’s much more laidback Kiosk is in the same building) with characterful walls that bear the imprint of Pest’s great 19th-century floods. It’s a grand yet homey room for indulging in seasonally evolving eight- and 13-course menus (there are vegan options, too) conceived by chef Kornél Kaszás. Bespoke crockery and glassware buoy Russian salad draped in egg-white cream and a generous dollop of sturgeon caviar as well as a zucchini-hemp seed-lime ragout and ethereal brioche dusted with freeze-dried raspberry. It’s a meal evocative of the long-gone Austro-Hungarian Empire days yet somehow feels completely fresh and relevant. Best for: seasonal-driven shared plates in a cosy neighbourhood setting Seven motley friends, including nightlife veteran Gyuri Takács, chef Norbi Piszkor, tattoo artist Robi Borbás, musician Ádám Schwarcz , content creator Barna Turai, and actors Bence Brasch and Dávid Miller banded together to bring Galamb Vendéglátás to life. The restaurant, located in the shadow of the pretty park Károlyi Kert, focuses on seasonally, locally sourced ingredients that Piszkor transforms into the likes of celery shawarma with green apple salsa and labneh and beef tartare crowned with from-scratch Japanese mayonnaise and mustard ice cream. Such an eclectic group of visionaries, though, translates to a cinematic atmosphere. Sleek wood paneling, splashes of red, and natural wines make Galamb just the place to hole up in until bedtime. Address: Henszlmann Imre u. 9,Budapest 1053 Best for: casual nights out that satisfy Vietnamese cravings Dish to order: cheeseburger spring rolls Budapest denizens felt the void when Krisztián Huszár closed his thrilling Vietnamese-Hungarian mash-up Vietnámigulyás in Buda earlier this year. But that’s good news for the team at Zen Eatery. Co-chefs and co-owners Pisti Szelei and Luu Trong Vinh are acolytes of Huszár’s, and they’ve instilled their greenery-brightened restaurant with a similar, yet distinctive kind of fusion magic. After moving into a larger space on central Liszt Ferenc square, complete with a shady summer terrace ripe for spectating, more and more intrigued pedestrians have taken notice of the specialities, like a comforting smash burger-stuffed bao, rich, cheesy donkatsu tamed with cucumber salad, and a hearty beef cheek paired with Korean rice cakes and a gochujang-infused sweet, creamy Hungarian vadas sauce. Paprika never goes out of fashion in Budapest, but locals can’t get enough of flavours like ginger and coconut either. Address: Liszt Ferenc tér 10., földszint 16., Budapest 1061 Best for: a relaxed café break bolstered by fresh-baked goods Dish to order: walnut-vanilla cream bucka The Brothers Buda, Tamás and Gábor, first launched Termelő as a pop-up, so locals have long been acquainted with their sold-out confections. With the arrival of a proper brick-and-mortar shop in a prime District IX location, then, the siblings are ready to show off their baking savvy to a wider public. Loaves of sourdough bread, sesame seed-strewn bagels, cinnamon buns—a nod to their time spent in Scandinavia—and brawny walnut and vanilla cream bucka are all reasons to chill out in the airy café adorned with black and white tiles, sconces, and large windows. Termelő joins a long list of stellar Budapest bakeries, including Déryné Kenyér, Artizán, and Läget. But it stands out because of Tamás and Gábor’s energy. The enthusiasm and ambition they showcased in a slew of previous roving events now materialises in a stylish permanent hangout for the community. Website: instagram.com/termelo_budapest/ Best for: friendly, contemporary tasting menu outing Just 20 minutes southwest of Budapest’s city centre is Budaörs, a commercial hub and residential suburb that is home to the compelling Rutin. At precisely 7 p.m., Dávid and Fanni Pallag—he’s the chef, she curates the wine list—invite guests into their intimate bistro, a former pub, for a 10-course tasting menu that shifts with the seasons. Fond memories of the Hungarian kitchen fuel Dávid’s modern-day interpretations. Here, classic gulyás, for instance, is invigorated with homemade pastrami, paprikás with silky nokedli (egg noodle dumplings) swaps out traditional chicken for mushroom, and charcoal-grilled pigeon is accompanied by a stuffed rendition of dödölle, the potato dumpling beloved in western Hungary’s Őrség region. Rutin is certainly fine dining, but creations like a caramelised, sugar-sprinkled bread soaked in liquid cheesecake for hours elevate recipes of yore, proving that nostalgia is now more sought after than pretence.

item.title: SALES: 8 best Afghan restaurants in London for your next culinary adventure
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Afghan food is undoubtedly delicious. From delicate mantu dumplings stuffed with minced meat and smothered in garlicky yoghurt to enormous platters of Kabuli Pulao, fragrant rice piled high with tender lamb and sweet raisins, the cuisine is full of rich flavours. Then there are the smoky charcoal-grilled kebabs and gently spiced, slow-cooked stews, best scooped up with freshly baked naan and washed down with glasses of doogh, a salty yoghurt drink flavoured with mint. Yet despite all this, Afghan restaurants remain relatively overlooked in a city that prides itself on eating its way around the world. A handful of newer openings are beginning to change that. In Leyton, recently opened Azra has embraced the sort of polished interiors and small-plate dining that Londoners have become rather fond of. Elsewhere, Cue Point is taking a more unconventional approach, combining traditional Afghan flavours with the smoky, slow-cooked techniques of Texan barbecue. Many of the capital's older Afghan restaurants, however, are found in areas with established Afghan communities, particularly Harrow in northwest London, with others scattered across Islington and Holloway. These are often reassuringly old-school affairs, where Afghan flags hang proudly on the walls, televisions chatter away in the background and the furniture might not have received much attention from an interior designer. But in an age when Instagrammable interiors have become, rather unfairly, something of a prerequisite for a good restaurant, don't be put off by a little decorative eccentricity. The cooking is superb, with enormous portions and family recipes passed down through generations. From neighbourhood stalwarts to smart new openings, these are the best Afghan restaurants in London.
