item.title: SALES: 11 best bars in Budapest, from ruin pubs to cocktail spots
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
I moved to Budapest more than 11 years ago, and I remember the disappointment I felt upon discovering there were only a few bars to savour artfully made cocktails in. So, I rekindled an old love for wine – not especially challenging in a country that produces countless beautiful bottles – and sipped shots of pálinka (Hungarian fruit brandy) on vintage chairs in ruin pubs, a once clamoured-for phenomenon that is fast fading, while waiting for the kind of spirituous bar scene I craved and often wrote about to flourish. Thankfully, I can report this moment has arrived. It happened slowly, with promising new ventures making a notable impression and enticing locals to expand their imbibing repertoire with tried-and-true drinks and bold originals alike. Organically, it developed, coinciding with the waning backpacker culture once synonymous with Budapest that has given way to something more polished. Successful bar owners are conceiving complementary spin-offs, hotel bars are becoming destinations, and posh interiors are becoming an essential part of a bar’s narrative. Cocktails are booming in Budapest, and here’s where to find them – along with a few consistently alluring watering holes for oenophiles and beer nerds. Drink to order: mulled wine in the winter; minőségi bor (quality wine) the rest of the year All Budapest itineraries should include an obligatory stop at Szimpla Kert, the city’s original labyrinthine ruin bar. Csendes Létterem, however, is the one to hole up in. Refuel here after a wander through the Hungarian National Museum and plunge into a wondrous world where a bicycle hangs from the ceiling, walls are covered in scribbles, and tattered dolls mingle with vintage lampshades. Amid the peculiar assemblage of objects are chandeliers and regal columns, hints the space was once home to the grand 19th-century Café Fiume. Just up the street is Károlyi Kert, one of Budapest’s loveliest parks, and between spring and autumn, the bar’s outdoor sibling, Csendes Társ, magically beckons at the entrance with spritzers. Address: Ferenczy István u. 5, Budapest 1053 Best for: wine lovers in search of laid-back neighbourhood vibes Drink to order: Weingartner Olaszrizling from Somló It’s in an out-of-the-way location, but that is part of Cintányéros’s appeal. Imre Molnár debuted his timeless, old photograph-bedecked corner tavern in 2016, and neighbours have been grateful ever since. House wines (an Olaszrizling from Balaton and a Villány rosé are always waiting) are ladled into carafes or incorporated into spritzers that pave the way to the hearty Bókay, the signature Reuben sandwich. There are offbeat Hungarian natural offerings too, such as Szóló’s “Levegő,” a Furmint from Tokaj, and the “Glou-Glou” Kékfrankos-Zweigelt blend made by Unger in Kőszeg. Relish a glass from the intimate mezzanine heightened by the transporting sounds of live piano music below. On the first Wednesday of the month, partake in Borász Fogadóórája, where Molnár welcomes in a natural wine producer to chat and crack open new and rare vintages tableside. Best for: a departure from typical District VII madness Tiny Cooldown is a much-needed addition to rowdy District VII, satiating the influx of revellers craving a more civilised experience in the neighbourhood. Bartender Sebestyén Mihalik is inspired by the onslaught of minimalist bars in Japan, translating to a calming atmosphere, complete with shoji screen and immaculately carved ice. The playful Stard*st menu fusing cheap dad jokes with celebrity culture is a surprise, then. Take the Post Malone, a crowd-pleasing clarified cocktail with rum, coconut, and cantaloupe unapologetically garnished with a bubblegum tattoo, or the Ricky Martini. This quenching highball twist bringing together ricotta-infused vodka, tomato water, thyme cordial, and a touch of truffle is tricked out with a thermometer indicating a fever. On their nights off, bartenders frequently stop by Cooldown, lending it the air of a see-and-be-seen industry night. Best for: date night in the company of reimagined classic libations Inside the centrally located Kempinski Hotel Corvinus Budapest, Balázs Molnár (partner with Boutiq Bar’s Zoltán Nagy on Moena vermouth) presides over Blue Fox the Bar. The globe-trotting Molnár previously worked in London, Hong Kong, and Sydney, and he brings a cosmopolitan flair to the elegant boîte buoyed by glowing cobalt and mirrored columns. Alongside classics like a whiskey sour reinterpreted with fig and cream, concept menus reel in the curious. Dubbed Blueprint, the current one explores the tenets of hospitality through drinks like the Terra Verde with gin, lime, celery, and for a savoury lift, olive oil. There’s also the Zen Garden, a Japanese-style shochu, red shiso, and yuzu long drink that makes for an intriguing aperitif before Chicken Kiev at the hotel’s recently renovated ÉS Bisztró. Address: Erzsébet tér 7-8, Budapest 1051 Best for: an upscale post-sightseeing break Gawking is mandatory at the Párisi Udvar Hotel Budapest, part of Hyatt’s Unbound Collection. Rather than simply passing through the property to look up at the magnificent crystal dome, Bar Henry is an invitation to take pleasure in the ornate ambience of this one-time shopping arcade and bank headquarters designed in the early 20th century with carved stone, Zsolnay ceramics, and stained glass. The bar is an ode to its architect Henrik Schmahl, who brilliantly layered Art Nouveau, Gothic, and Middle Eastern influences, and the cocktails a celebration of the building’s heritage. A mix of cognac, carrot, vanilla, cinnamon, and nutmeg sparks a Moorish Reverie, while mezcal, cold-brew coffee, cherry, citrus, and tonka-almond milk foam recapture the Treasury After Midnight. Address: Ferenciek tere 10, Budapest 1053 Best for: craft beer geeks with a penchant for production methods Drink to order: Antimatter imperial coffee stout Budapest’s craft beer fans enjoy nights at Hops and Hopaholic but unlike those standbys, the multi-pronged, subterranean Gravity Brewing is at once a working brewery, experimental lab, and taproom. On Saturdays, the public is encouraged to tour the former bunker and get a glimpse inside those small-batch operations, even tasting samples straight from the tanks. But the rest of the week, the minimalist bar done up in whitewashed brick on the other side of the glass is the focal point. Slide into a banquette and choose from continuously rotating tap selections, like the dark chocolatey Antimatter imperial coffee stout or Lunasa oaked Irish red. Pay special attention to Gravity’s Prototype series, highlighting such limited-edition brews as a quince-peppercorn saison and blackberry ryewine. Best for: eye-catching cocktails in a complementary duo of moody spaces Zoltán Nagy opened Boutiq Bar, the blue-door bolthole credited with introducing craft cocktails to Budapest, in 2008. It’s classy and dimly lit, and despite other like-minded bars that have sprouted in the city, it remains a favourite for consistently well-wrought drinks accompanied by cordial service. Order a Riserva Negroni showcasing the double-aged expression of Unicum, the Hungarian herbal liqueur, and Moena vermouth—the brand the restless Nagy launched with fellow Budapest bartender Balázs Molnár—and conversations are sure to organically flow. Downstairs is home to Pink Pony Club, another more casual concept founded in 2019 by Molnár and now helmed by Diego Rastellà. At this sexy dive bar, the Bruschettini, a gin martini spawned from distilled bruschetta, and the Salmon Says, an unlikely amalgamation of Scotch whisky, Nutella, and smoked salmon, illuminate Rastellà’s wildly imaginative mind. Best for: experimental cocktails in a fashionable setting Elysian’s Máté Szabó is ambitious. His bar, smack in the middle of raucous surroundings, is the antithesis of shots and mayhem. Here, patrons escape to a two-sided bar counter beneath a mess of driftwood that washed up on the Danube and mull over a range of ever-changing, seasonal cocktails. Szabó constantly plays with fermentation and those preserved ingredients emerge in clever tipples like the signature bloody mary that marries vodka with shiitake mushroom and paprika, an especially apt pairing with fries plunked into bloody mary ketchup. Embracing local products is also important to the Elysian ethos, exemplified in such decidedly Hungarian concoctions as a Hanky Panky riff combining Misi’s gin, Moena vermouth, raspberry honey, and Unicum Orange Bitter. A glamorous aura pervades Múzsa, the centrepiece of the Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace’s stained glass-adorned lobby lounge. During the afternoon, tea is served on handpainted Hungarian Herend porcelain in the swanky Art Nouveau-style room, but in the evening, all eyes are on the shimmering bar overseen by the newly installed Federico Daniele, who previously worked at Drink Kong in Rome and Boadas Cocktails in Barcelona. In the past, Múzsa cocktail menus have paid homage to formative memories, muses, and modern art. For the latest one, currently under development, Daniele and his team are putting Hungarian ingredients in the spotlight and drawing from the hotel’s own trove of colourful stories. One of the high points? A lineup of frozen martinis. Address: Széchenyi István tér 5-6, Budapest 1051 Best for: conceptual cocktails in a mysterious setting First came Hotsy Totsy, the subterranean bar in District VII that’s always a blast. Crowned in a vaulted brick ceiling, it’s reminiscent of a speakeasy, with drinks hatched in honour of such New York landmarks as The Dakota apartment building and The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Then the team unveiled Lilith, a snug, dark room mere minutes away named for the mythological figure symbolic of emancipation. The menu, a tour through seven feminine archetypes, takes the form of tarot cards, prompting guests to deliberate over the umami-forward Lilitu with dark rum, beetroot, dill, soy, and vinegar, or the more delicate, floral Temptress, brought to life with berry-flavored gin, grenadine, rosewater, and orange honey. Sometimes, the light shifts to a deep, saturated red, making the space even more seductive to passersby. Address: Rumbach Sebestyén u. 7, Budapest 1075 Beef Wellington feasts unfold at Felix Kitchen & Bar, and then in-the-know diners head downstairs to the loungey Hide for nightcaps. The neo-renaissance building, designed by acclaimed Hungarian architect Ybl Miklós in 1875, is a former pumping station that purified water for the nearby Royal Palace, and Hide proudly alludes to that history with its well-preserved structural walls and soft arches enveloped in an amber sheen. It’s a theatrical backdrop for delighting in a coveted DJ set and a drinks list steered by Gergely Piller, formerly of Salmon Guru Dubai. Retreat to one of the hidden nooks with a Corteza Spritz melding Italian and Asian flavours of amaretto, sesame oil, mango, and honeydew, or the dark and spiced rum BudapesTT, rife with date, coffee, cocoa, and salted caramel notes, and it’s akin to spending the night in a private club. Address: Ybl Miklós tér 9, Budapest 1013

item.title: SALES: 12 Gifts for the Outdoorsy Person Who Already Has All the Gear
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy Black Diamond RockLock Magnetron Carabiner Dale of Norway 1994 Lillehammer Wool Sweater Camp Snap CS8 Point and Shoot Video Camcorder Ripstop by the Roll DIY Zipper Pouch Kit Some might argue that the person who already has everything is the hardest to shop for. But we disagree. It’s an opportunity to throw practicality out the window and find something so offbeat, clever, or downright whimsical that they’d never think to buy it themselves. That’s what makes shopping for them so fun. Consider it your chance to give something unexpected, such as the 12 gifts below. They might have all the gear, but have they ever made their own gear? When the weather is crappy and the daylight wanes, this DIY zipper pouch is just the thing to keep them busy. Ripstop by the Roll provides the Dyneema fabric, YKK coil zipper and slider, and drawcord (thread not included), and it’s up to them to put everything together. Choose from three sizes. For the nature lover who always points out the tiniest alpine flowers on hikes, this pocket-sized notebook for pressing botanical treasures is the perfect stocking stuffer. The cream-colored pages fold accordion-style for a double layer so moisture doesn’t leak through, and a tight elastic band wraps around the whole journal for secure compression. Who knew a triangle of fabric could be so versatile? Made from Polartec Alpha microfleece, this scarf is cozy enough to boost warmth but slim enough to slide under layers on the coldest days. It’s wide enough to wrap multiple times around the neck, or once around the shoulders or head. The edges are bound in one of Skida’s signature patterns—leopard print or florals—for a subtle boost of personality. It’s back! After a six-year hiatus, your climbing-obsessed loved one will be delighted to know this beloved magnetic locking carabiner is in production again. Unlike locking carabiners that require users to twist a screw tight, the Magnetron locks automatically when the gate is closed. The first rerun sold out, but restocks arrived just in time for gifting season. Published in 2025, this gorgeous coffee table book presents magazines, catalogs, and other printed materials from the past 100 years of the outdoor industry. Iconic brands featured include Snow Peak, The North Face, and Columbia, with a foreword from photographer Chris Burkard. Anyone who’s a nerd about gear will leave this book out, flip through its 384 pages obsessively, and return to it for endless inspiration. The Hex 2.0 is a chair, a stadium seat, a sleeping pad, and a kneeling mat, all in one. With both straps clipped together to create a supportive seat, the eight-millimeter high-density cored closed-cell foam provides insulation and comfort off the ground. A DWR coating ensures moisture from the wet ground or bleachers doesn’t seep up and ruin your day. It’s compact and lightweight enough to roll up and carry in a daypack or toss in the car for a tailgate. We guarantee the recipient already owns a camp mug—or two or three. They probably wouldn’t spend $110 on another one themselves. But that’s exactly why you should. Snow Peak’s matching golden set, inspired by autumn leaves, is equally at home around the campfire or on the kitchen counter, making everyday tea and coffee feel a little more special. Everyone has a camera in their pocket, but how often do those videos make it out of the camera roll? The Camp Snap camcorder gives everyday moments the nostalgic treatment of an old-school home movie. Without a playback screen, the person behind the lens has to trust their instincts, just like back in the day. But a USB-C connection makes transferring footage easy. Perhaps this is the encouragement your loved one needs to finally make that ski film. Surely your loved one already has a pair of tried-and-true trail shoes. But do they have these trail shoes? The collaboration between Québec footwear brand Norda and climbing gear maker Black Diamond was one of the year’s most exciting partnerships, and this limited-edition shoe is its crown jewel. Here’s your chance to give someone something they might have admired from afar but wouldn’t necessarily splurge on themselves. All their gear has to go somewhere, and hopefully in an organized manner. The RUX Waterproof Duffel Box keeps everything contained in one durable, grab-and-go bag for impromptu trips to wherever. Its zipperless roll-top design expands or compresses to accommodate whatever they’re packing, while interior soft organizers keep smaller essentials from getting lost in the shuffle. The 840-denier TPU-coated nylon on the outside is absolutely bombproof. Sorry, Grandma. We’ve got the knitwear covered this year. Dale of Norway re-created its 1994 Olympic ski sweater with the same Norwegian craftsmanship, but a thinner, softer 100 percent wool yarn in a unisex fit. This cozy layer is also a little piece of ski history for the powder chaser and forecast checker in your life. Collaborations make especially good gifts, particularly when they’re limited to just 500 pieces. Japanese retailer BEAMS teamed up with REI to reimagine a parka inspired by the co-op’s original 1986 design, unearthed in its archives. For the person who loves a good vintage find, this is about as good as it gets.

item.title: REVIEW: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro Review: A Better Tablet Rises From the Fire's Ashes
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, starting at $499.99, kicks off the divorce party I've been waiting for. It marks the end of Amazon's Fire tablet lineup, which locked users into Amazon’s closed ecosystem. Although that may be fine for those invested in Amazon Prime and its services, some prefer a more open platform. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro represents a huge shift; it still includes all the Amazon apps and content you want, but now lets you seek out and use third-party apps from the Google Play Store. The Tablet 12 Pro combines Amazon's best-ever hardware with excellent performance, great battery life, and a flexible reading experience, with all the apps you want or need at a price you can afford. It's a great turnaround from Amazon and our new Editors' Choice for midrange Android tablets. Tablet designs have always been a snoozefest, and the 12 Pro is no different. It sticks to the run-of-the-mill rectangular slab look, featuring flat, rounded-corner edges and a matte back panel. It feels sturdy and well-built, thanks to its unibody aluminum casing. It's not immune to fingerprints, but the Graphite finish—the 12 Pro's sole color option—does an impressive job of disguising smudges, even under direct light. The 12 Pro measures 10.66 by 7.24 by 0.26 inches (HWD) and weighs 1.21 pounds. Pitted against a comparable Android tablet, the $549.99 Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE (10.01 by 6.53 by 0.24 inches, 1.09 pounds) is more compact across the board. The entry-level $449 Apple iPad (9.79 by 7.07 by 0.28 inches, 1.05 pounds) is shorter and narrower, but thicker and lighter. My first thought when I picked up the 12 Pro is that it's quite hefty. It's fine while navigating the tablet with both hands, but holding it one-handed for nighttime reading gets tiring after about 10 minutes. If reading ebooks is your primary activity, I'd get a lighter Kindle. The Alexa Tablet 11 (9.97 by 6.49 by 0.27 inches, 1.03 pounds) and Alexa Tablet 8 (8.23 by 5.22 by 0.31 inches, 0.73 pounds) models are thicker than the 12 Pro, but they're lighter and more portable, so they might be a better choice if you want something more featherweight. The 12 Pro has thick black bezels that frame it, which I don't mind because it gives my thumbs a place to rest. Holding it in landscape orientation, you'll find a front-facing camera on the top bezel. Flip it over, and you'll see the main camera in the top-right corner. You'll find two speaker grilles and a USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 port on the short edges. The smaller Alexa slates have USB-C 2.0 ports that don't support external monitors and offer slower transfer speeds. The other short edge holds a set of speaker grilles, a power button that doubles as a responsive and reliable fingerprint reader, and a trigger for Alexa. Pogo pins for attaching to the optional Alexa Tablet Pro Keyboard ($149.99) line the bottom long edge. The 12 Pro has an IP52 rating, which means it can withstand dust and minor splashes, but not submersion. The S10 FE has a much better IP68 rating; it's dust-tight and can survive about three feet of water for 30 minutes. The 11th-gen iPad doesn't have an IP rating, making it more susceptible to dust and liquids. The 12 Pro features Corning-based glass, though it’s not branded as traditional Gorilla Glass. Instead, Amazon partnered with Corning specifically for its nanomatte anti-glare finish. The S10 FE is shielded with Gorilla Glass 3, which offers decent scratch resistance. In contrast, the iPad has a fingerprint-resistant oleophobic coating. Amazon offers two display options for the 12 Pro: a standard display on the $499.99 model, and a nanomatte finish on the $549.99 model. I tested the nanomatte version, which reminds me of the nanotexture display on the iPad Pro. I am in tactile heaven when I run my fingers across the display. The 12 Pro's screen feels less like slick glass and more like high-quality stationery paper. The 12 Pro has a 12-inch display with a 2,800-by-1,840-pixel resolution at 280 pixels per inch (ppi). The Tablet 11 and Tablet 8 models offer 11-inch and 8-inch displays, respectively. I didn't need to read the spec sheet to know the 12 Pro has a 120Hz display; the ultra-smooth, responsive touch screen gave it away. The S10 FE has a smaller 10.9-inch display; its 2,304-by-1,440-pixel resolution and 90Hz refresh rate fall short of the 12 Pro's higher-resolution and smoother experience. The 11-inch iPad has a 2,360-by-1,640-pixel resolution screen at 264ppi. Both the Amazon and Apple tablets put out 500 nits of brightness, but the 12 Pro delivers crisper, more razor-sharp text and visual clarity. In the top-left corner of the screen, there's a widget that cycles through date, weather, and time cards, my last-watched Prime Video show, and my latest Kindle read. Tap on Continue Reading to pop right back into your current book. When you do this, the screen seamlessly switches to a warmer, eye-friendly display theme. If the default setting isn't your vibe, you can choose between two other display themes: Color Paper for a softened, printed-paper look, or Ink Paper for a distraction-free grayscale experience. I took the 12 Pro for a spin outside and needed to crank the brightness slider all the way up, but the panel held its ground against daylight far better than glossy glass. Reading is when I appreciate the screen's 3:2 aspect ratio the most; the extra screen height makes reading feel spacious, giving words and margins plenty of room to breathe. The nanomatte screen eliminates harsh light and direct reflections, allowing me to enjoy a glare-free video viewing experience. The picture, whether I was watching outdoors or indoors, looks subdued, with dark scenes lacking punch. The matte finish fends off reflections, but colors lose a bit of their pop. This is par for the course. Videos are often letterboxed on the 3:2 screen, but it doesn't distract me. If you dislike black bars when watching movies, go for the Tablet 11, which has a 16:10 aspect ratio. Overall, the display is fine for video, but if you’re a stickler for rich contrast and punchy visuals, you’re better off saving $50 and sticking with the standard model, especially if you'll spend most of your time with it indoors. MediaTek’s 4nm Dimensity 8400 chip powers the S12 Pro. At $499.99, the base, non-nanomatte 12 Pro comes with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. I tested the base nanomatte model, which has the same specs for $549.99, though you can upgrade to 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage for $679.99. The S10 FE starts at $549.99 and comes with a Samsung Exynos 1580 processor, 8GB of RAM, and 128GB of storage, but you can upgrade that to 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage for an extra $120. The 11th-gen iPad, featuring the A16 chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro, costs $449 for 128GB of storage, $549 for 256GB, or $749 for 512GB; all configurations come with 6GB of RAM. On paper, the 12 Pro gives you the most bang for your buck by pairing 8GB of RAM with 128GB of storage; the S10 FE offers the least, charging an extra $50 for the same configuration. However, specs only tell half the story. I put both tablets through our usual benchmark tests to see which tablet packs the most real-world oomph. On Geekbench 7, the 12 Pro delivered scores of 1,460 (single-core) and 6,310 (multi-core). The 11th-gen iPad fared better on the single-core test (2,479), but fell behind on the multi-core test (4,352). We only tested the S10 FE+, but it has the same processor as the S10 FE. Compared with the 12 Pro, the Samsung tablet underperformed with scores of 1,358 and 3,886. Compared with its rivals, the 12 Pro delivers more muscle for multi-threaded workloads. On the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme benchmark, which tests the GPU for graphics performance, the 12 Pro notched an overall score of 3,344 at 20.02 frames per second (fps). This beats the iPad's score of 2,599 at 15.6fps. On the PCMark Work 3.1 benchmark, which tests productivity tasks such as web browsing and document editing, the 12 Pro delivered a score of 15,648. This outmuscles the S10 FE, which could only muster 13,361. In the real world, I played the graphics-intensive Genshin Impact set at 60 frames per second, and gameplay was a slick and smooth experience. Whether I was running around the map or deep in combat while battling enemies, there were no stutters, noticeable frame drops, or visual lag. The 12 Pro sports a 9,000mAh battery that Amazon claims can last for 16 hours of video playback. On the PCMag battery test, which involves looping a 1080p video over Wi-Fi with the screen's brightness at 100%, the 12 Pro lasted 7 hours and 33 minutes on a single charge—just shy of the Samsung tablet's 7 hours and 45 minutes. However, the 12 Pro managed to beat the iPad's 6 hours and 43 minutes. After connecting the 12 Pro to a compatible charger (50W), I was disappointed with its slow charging. It only reached 13% after 15 minutes and 35% after 30 minutes. It took 2 hours and 36 minutes to fill its tank to 100%. Plan ahead before you take it out of the house. The 12 Pro supports Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3. Amazon doesn't offer a cellular configuration, so you'll be relying entirely on Wi-Fi if you plan to use it on the go. Positioned next to my home's Wi-Fi 6 router, the 12 Pro reached maximum speeds of 307Mbps down and 197Mbps up. An iPad Air tested in the same spot delivered similar speeds: 310Mbps down and 151Mbps up. At the edge of my Wi-Fi network, the 12 Pro reached 77.1Mbps down and 20.9Mbps up, while the iPad hit 185Mbps down and 77.0Mbps up. The 12 Pro features a Dolby Atmos-tuned, quad-speaker setup. It's on the quieter side, not climbing above 75dB during testing. I don't care for the sound quality. PCMag's test track, The Knife's "Silent Shout," sounded tinny, as if it was playing inside of a box. There's a dedicated Dolby Atmos app that lets you switch between four presets: Dynamic, Movie, Music, and Voice. The Music preset gave the tune a slight push forward and widened the stereo field, but it still felt flat and hollow. The iPad provides a richer audio experience. The 12 Pro comes with two cameras: a 13MP rear camera and an 8MP selfie shooter. Cameras on tablets are usually an afterthought, and that's pretty much the case with the 12 Pro. I took the 13MP rear camera for a spin and noticed that the lens doesn't perform well in direct sunlight. The limited dynamic range meant that the flower's pink petals (below) blew out into bright white patches. The camera handled this leaf much better, capturing its rich, orangey-red tone and sharp surface details without blowing out the exposure. The sharpness tails off a bit toward the outer edges. In this shot of a bridge, an aggressive lens-flare streak cuts through the middle, destroying the photo's contrast and creating a washed-out look. The main camera supports up to 2x digital zoom, but the quality drops significantly. The zoomed-in photo delivered a soft, hazy shot with smudged detail and low contrast. The 8MP selfie camera is OK. It captures good facial detail and renders accurate colors. However, step into direct sunlight, and you're immediately met with blown-out skin tones and uneven shadows. Video recording tops out at 1080p on both the front and rear cameras. You can toggle between two aspect ratios: 16:9 and 4:3. Plus, you can set a timer up to 10 seconds, allowing you to position yourself in the frame if you want. Videos aren't the sharpest, and they tend to be highly saturated, which may appeal to you if you prefer punchy, vibrant colors. Video quality is decent for casual video calls. There's a permanently docked Ask Alexa button sitting at the bottom-right corner of the home screen. I'm more familiar with Gemini, but my experience with Alexa was a pleasant surprise. To test it, I scrolled to a photo of the iPhone Duo in a PCMag article. After waking the assistant with "Hey Alexa," I asked, "Which gadget is this, and is there a better recommendation for someone seeking something thin and light?" Alexa correctly identified the Apple foldable before suggesting that the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the best option for me. I also asked it to identify a dish from a photo and walk me through the recipe; it instantly recognized the Shakshuka and broke down a quick cooking guide. If you want Alexa to "see" the entirety of an article, not just what's visible on the screen, you'll want to use Silk, Amazon's browser. In Silk, Alexa does an impressive job at summarizing articles and answering questions based on what you're reading. If AI is a priority for you, the 12 Pro's deep Alexa integration gives it an edge over the entry-level iPad (which lacks Apple Intelligence) and the S10 FE (which has a limited suite of AI tools). The 12 Pro runs on Android 16, and Amazon promises an impressive seven years of OS and security upgrades. This commitment is far superior to the nebulous promises Amazon made in the past and puts the 12 Pro on even footing with the iPad and even Samsung's Galaxy tablets. Amazon's former FireOS was often a restrictive experience; I'm relieved that the 12 Pro frees me from the confines of the Amazon ecosystem. It still comes preloaded with Amazon’s core apps (e.g., Kindle, Prime Video, and Audible), but they now coexist with Google’s suite of apps, including Gmail, Maps, YouTube, and the all-important Play Store. You now get the best of both worlds: a little bit of Amazon and a sweet helping of Google. I dig the multitasking features that let me drag any app into split-screen mode. Taking a page out of Samsung's DeX mode or Apple's Stage Manager, there's also Desktop Windowing, which features a taskbar at the bottom and lets you juggle multiple floating apps. During testing, I was able to run up to five windows simultaneously, with full freedom to resize and reposition them however I wanted. This is so much better. Amazon sent me a stylus and a keyboard, but it's important to note that neither ships with the 12 Pro. Amazon offers a tablet-and-keyboard bundle that starts at $599.99 for the standard model; you'll have to spend an extra $50 for a nanomatte upgrade. Throw in the stylus that Amazon calls the Alexa Tablet Pro Pen, and that'll set you back another $89.99. The keyboard set comes in two pieces: a protective back shell with a built-in kickstand and a detachable magnetic keyboard deck. The typing experience exceeded my expectations; the Chiclet-style keys are addictively clicky and responsive. The keyboard features a handful of helpful keys, including a button that summons Alexa and one that opens the Writing Assist toolbar. If you highlight some text and tap the Writing Assist key, you'll see the following options: proofread, rewrite, elaborate, concise, key points, emojify, professional, witty, casual. The core tools handle the basics—fixing grammar, rephrasing, expanding, trimming, and summarizing—while the tone options adjust your voice to fit the room. Pairing the stylus required me to snap it into one exact spot on the top bezel. It wouldn't register anywhere else, even though the tablet has magnetic sweet spots all around the frame. The pen sports a sleek matte finish, a comfortable, weighted grip, and a side button that lets you switch to the eraser instantly. There aren't any preinstalled drawing apps, but I downloaded Clip Studio Paint to test it out by sketching a cinnamon bun. The tilt sensitivity made shading the pastry's curves feel natural. Plus, the low latency was impressive. My favorite feature, by far, is Find My Pen, which triggers a chime to help you hunt down your pen. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. item.title: REVIEW: GMKtec EVO-X5 Pro mini PC review: I tested large LLMs on this machine and the results and speed were impressive
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
There’s no doubt this is a fantastic-looking, high-performing machine, but it comes at a steep price. Tested with office and creative applications in a traditional way, this machine just feels like overkill. However, harness the power of AI with companion apps such as Visual Studio or DaVinci Resolve, and what’s possible completely offline is mind-blowing. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The EVO-X5 packs in the latest Strix Halo CPU, and while the updates to the specifications of the Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 processor over the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 may look modest, when you give it the additional boost of 196GB of unified memory and the internal space for up to 24TB of storage, you suddenly have a machine whose abilities far exceed the superb EVO-X3 I reviewed recently. Like so many of these small machines, it’s hard to believe the power it contains when it arrives. The box is small and relatively discreet, a departure from the large, powerful gaming and AI workstations I usually associate with its computing power. Part of the reason for that size reduction is that this is the processing hub, and while the AMD Radeon 8065S graphics will see you through a decent bit of gaming, if you want that full GPU power alongside what’s on offer with the CPU, you’ll need to break out to an external GPU option. This distinction makes the machine's intended use clear. You can use it on its own as a powerful workstation, handling everything from office day tasks to video and image editing, and even 3D work. You can also rack it alongside additional EVO-X5 Pros to build an almighty AI personal data centre, with features such as the OOB, which lets you access and control the machine even if it’s mid-blue-screen or terminal crash. However, professional IT skills will inevitably also be needed. On a smaller scale, and in the way that I’ve checked this machine out in this review, is to check the day-to-day function first. Is this $5000 machine good enough to run Microsoft Windows, Office, Adobe Creative Suite, edit images, video, and audio, and all the base functions a powerful machine in the office or studio needs to do, especially at that price? But to go deeper: if this machine is going to cost almost double today’s pretty decent workstations, why should I pay all that extra money for a machine like this? Am I just paying for the latest AI-enhanced CPUs, or is there more to it? Can the machine's capabilities offset that cost? To put it to the test, I’ve run through all the usual benchmarks and real-world tests, but after testing a good volume of AI headline-leading mini PCs, I want to see if it can take on a little more. For instance, can it not only code a straight site, but also build a site from designs? What is the image-generation capability, and can it really run a 300B LLM without stalling? What I’ve noticed with some smaller mini PCs recently is that while they meet the specs and perform impressively, most hit their limits pretty quickly. However, with far more unified RAM than most, this machine has plenty of headroom. The main test for me here is: can it effectively edit video in DaVinci Resolve? While my workstation can do this, it takes time, and a couple of the machines I’ve looked at recently have hit their limits with that kind of processing. This looks to be a formidable machine among the best mini PCs I've reviewed, and one that will suit many looking into the use of AI in their day-to-day workflows. But all this power comes at a huge cost, and in balance, is this machine worth that price? GMKtec EVO-X5 Pro: Price and availability - How much does it cost? From £5,299 / $6,799 - Where can you get it? Directly from GMKtec or Amazon The machine is available in either a 2TB or 4TB version, with a $400 / £300 increase for the extra storage. CPU: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495, 16 cores/32 threads GPU: AMD Radeon 8065S, 40 RDNA 3.5 compute units RAM: 192GB LPDDR5X-8533 unified memory, non-upgradeable Storage: 2TB or 4TB PCIe 4.0 M.2 2280 SSD, three slots, up to 24TB total Front Ports: 2 x USB 3.2 Gen 2, 2 x USB4, 3.5mm audio, P-Mode button, CMOS reset Rear Ports: HDMI 2.1, 2 x USB4 v2 80Gbps, 2 x USB 2.0, 2 x 10GbE RJ-45 DASH, 3.5mm audio Power: 54W–120W selectable power modes, external power adapter The mini PC is getting bigger; although still compact, it sits somewhere between a small tower desktop and the more traditional mini PC size. The styling is also spot on, with the ability to lay the machine flat or upright depending on your desk space. It’s also nicely designed with an understated all-metal black finish, though GMKtec has included its usual feature: a green power button. This button features fingerprint recognition. The size, while not large, comes in at 221 × 80 × 195 mm, and in this review it sat neatly beside the monitor in a vertical position, taking up little desktop space. The weight at 2.5kg is substantial for a mini PC, but still far less than most workstations, so in a studio space or if you do need to take a machine out on site, this is a great option. The build quality is what you would expect at this price, with the all-metal black finish giving it a high-quality look and feel. Aesthetically, this is one of the best-looking mini PCs I’ve seen, while remaining quite understated. Another design point: while this machine can be used on its own, it's also designed to work alongside others, so its size and weight make it easy to connect to additional EVO-X5s if that’s what you or your business needs. The front layout is minimalistic, with a few essentials across the front. These include the P-Mode button, CMOS reset, two USB 3.2 Gen 2 ports, two USB4 ports, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and the power button. The P-Mode button is a physical button for switching between the power modes, which include silent, balanced and performance, with each adjusting the amount of power that the machine draws from 54W up to 120W, and as I went through the benchmark tests, I realised just how much difference this P-Mode button can make. That power draw helps explain the power brick that comes with the mini PC, which isn't much smaller than those of many standard mini PCs, but, as ever, can be tucked out of sight behind the machine. On the rear of the machine, there are plenty of ports, although again, as I’ve seen with these premium machines, the volume of connections is well balanced, with plenty of space given. Options include a 3.5mm audio out, HDMI 2.1, two USB4 v2, two USB 2.0, two 10GbE RJ45 DASH ports, power in and a Kensington lock slot. What interests me is that both RJ45 ports are 10GbE, enabling ultra-fast network speeds if your network can support them. One of the major issues with these smaller machines is keeping everything cool, and inside there is a network of cooling technologies and systems, with the vent structure visible across the back and top of the machine. As the workload increases, this machine does make some noise, but compared with workstations and servers, that noise is well controlled. Opening the box, the insides are neatly packed and much more complex in design than I would usually expect in a mini PC. However, the slots for the two additional M.2 sticks are relatively easy to access, with one being a standard M.2 2280 Key-M PCIe 4.0 x4 and the other being M.2 Key-M PCIe 4.0 x1. The RAM is unified, soldered to the motherboard, and not upgradable. The big news on the feature front for the EVO-X5 is the new Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495. While this only offers a slight uplift when it comes to the clock speed, the AI processing is where the real changes have been introduced, with the two headline points being the boost in the power of the integrated GPU and support for up to 196GB of RAM. There are, of course, other updates and speed boosts, but for AI processing, the 196GB is the headline, letting the machine hold larger language models in memory. GMKtec claims the 55 TOPS NPU, backed by the RAM boost, should let you run 320B LLMs locally. The integrated GPU also gets an upgrade to the Radeon 8065S, which retains the 40 RDNA 3.5 compute units but should boost gaming performance slightly. Likewise, the 196GB of RAM is a significant upgrade, especially since both the CPU and GPU share the memory. Again, as with the EVO-X3, the onboard memory is LPDDR5X but increases from 8000MT/s to 8533MT/s, boosting the bandwidth slightly for all that AI processing. In the creative field, connectivity is always important, and two features that instantly piqued my interest were the dual USB4 v2 80Gbps ports and 10GbE network ports. USB4 v2 is also 80Gbps, but it differs from Thunderbolt 5, which is stricter on some parameters. However, the documentation says you can connect an eGPU if needed. USB4 v2 also offers broad compatibility with external hard drives and SSDs, which are essential for storage, and it can even add two additional M.2 SSDs, boosting internal storage to 24TB. There are three M.2 2280 slots: two PCIe 4.0 x4 and one PCIe 4.0 x1. The 10GbE networking meant that, during the test, I could simply link the machine into the wired 10GbE network to access the UGreen INX6100. The transfer rates over the 10GbE network are fast enough for network video editing, and you can access and download all files stored on the NAS locally. The other point here is that while one system is AMD and the other is Intel, with the right LLM commands and setup, you can get the two working together, making it an ideal workflow option for sorting and tagging images, for instance. Alongside the impressive array of connection ports, there’s also Wi-Fi 7 to ensure fast internet connections. In testing, this also meant that when transferring files to the 3D printers, transfer rates for some of the larger files were exceptionally fast. When this speed was combined with the slicing speed within applications such as Bambu Studio, you can really start to see the machine’s potential. Two features that are interesting but are beyond the scope of this review are AMD DASH and TPM. AMD DASH stands for Desktop and Mobile Architecture for System Hardware and enables remote access and management. TPM stands for Trusted Platform Module and handles security. These are both aimed at enterprise users. GMKtec Claw and Herdsman come pre-installed and are both pretty decent. Herdsman is essentially along the same lines as LM Studio or Ollama, while GMKtec Claw features chat and the ability to set up automation tasks. They’re actually a great starting point, and both are evolving quickly, becoming more stable and making greater use of the full power of the machine, something that I noted with the EVO-X3 and the lack of connectivity to the NPU. Many applications, including those from Adobe, still use the GPU heavily for AI processing, although other applications are starting to use the dedicated AI processor. Cinebench R23 CPU Multi (Threads): 37055 Cinebench R23 CPU Single (Threads): 2082 Cinebench 2026 CPU Multi (Threads): 7666 Cinebench 2026 CPU Single (Threads): 465 Sky Diver: The EVO-X5 comes with Windows 11 Pro installed, and as ever, the final steps of the installation were needed before I could get started with installing the benchmark and real-world software applications. What was interesting here, and in common with the EVO-X3, was that GMKClaw and Herdsman were both pre-installed. Herdsman is essentially the local AI model management and inference platform. Essentially, it’s GMKtec’s option over LM Studio or Ollama, and offers plenty of options to download and manage LLMs locally. For most of the tests, I started with this option. Still, I switched to Lemonade, since I’m more familiar with the server and its ability to monitor token generation and use it for the local AI tests I wanted to run. Starting the tests, I ran through the usual array of Windows applications, including Microsoft Office, with a focus as ever on Word, to write this review, Excel, to store and query the results from the benchmark tests, and PowerPoint, to put together a series of photography lectures that I have running in the next week. Testing these applications on a machine at this level produced the real-world results I expected. All applications ran at speed with no lag, and switching quickly between them and online formatting tools was fast, keeping up with my editing speed without me ever having to wait for the applications to speed up. These real-world tests reflected the WEI score of 9.5, and again, that’s backed up by the PCMark score of 10,773, the highest score I’ve seen with any mini PC. Lightroom and Photoshop, like the Microsoft Office apps, just ran without issue. They were fast and responsive, and with well over 100 images, batch processing in Lightroom ran surprisingly through without issue or pause. Likewise, opening a selection of RAW files from Bridge into ACR, making amendments, and saving was equally quick. As I pushed the system with 4K video editing, it was clear that even without discrete graphics, performance was excellent. With the 2TB SSD, there was plenty of room to store and edit the footage locally, with the option to offload to the NAS once the edit was complete. What impressed me here was not only the ability to edit 4K footage from the Canon EOS R5C without slowdown, but also the ability to store that footage on the IDX6011 NAS and utilise the 10GbE network for editing. This meant that there was no need for a desktop SSD, as the speed over the network and with a local cache file was more than fast enough for all the work that I do. As the complexity of the edits increased, I noticed notable slowdowns when scrolling through the timeline and waiting for colour grade changes to render. However, it was still as fast as my workstation with discrete graphics. However, with the option to link in an eGPU, this would further boost video-editing potential, especially as you start to look at AI integrations with programs such as DaVinci Resolve. I started using Herdsman and located the largest model I could download and test. This was the DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 155.7GB. This left little actual headroom for the machine. However, the model worked, though progress was slow; when results came through chat questions, the answers were impressive. Still, even on this machine, the speed was too slow to be truly useful. Switching to Qwen3 30B-A3B at 17.2GB, the difference was instantly noticeable, with swift answers and useful abilities. However, I wanted to run a series of tests; first, I returned to Lemonade and the SDXL-Turbo model to create a 512 x 512 image of a dog on a beach. The image appeared almost instantly in just 2.5 seconds and was pretty decent. After experimenting a little more, I found the image generation speed and capability were the fastest I have seen so far. Although some images had slightly strange dog eyes, I switched models again and went with Z-Iage-Turbo. This larger 20GB model produced notably better results, though it took longer to render. The next test, and one that produces all sorts of results, was the website creation task. Here, Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF produced the site in 92 seconds, generating 4063 tokens at 45 tokens per second. This was just to generate the code, not to save and organise the files. Still, this was far faster than the EVO-X3 running the same task with the same source files. What was markedly different here was the quality of the site generated. This actually looked like a site, albeit slightly simple, that you could actually use as a point to develop or rework with AI. Looking through the results, the EVO-X5 clearly outperforms the EVO-X3. It’s not as large a step as I would have thought, but having that additional RAM does mean that larger and more complex models can be loaded, and their abilities are that much greater. However, many language models are designed to adapt to the hardware they’re running on. Still, running those same models on the EVO-X3 and EVO-X5 side by side shows that while everything but the RAM sees a small uplift, the EVO-X5 easily takes the edge in processing and result quality. Once again, model selection and the LLM Manager are all-important, as is the default token limit your machine can produce. Once you’ve found the model and increased the tokens through the command prompt for that model, things become more impressive. As ever, you also need to look for models that make full use of the NPU, rather than just falling back on the CPU and GPU. However, across the board, running local LLMs is more than possible, and while many of the speed differences between this and the older EVO-X3 seem small on paper, the real-world realisation of those speeds is marked in use. I found response times were generally faster, with slightly better responses, most notably in website creation. However, as ever, this partly comes down to the AI model's response at the time, and you will always get a different response from the same model on different systems. That said, the extra RAM does seem to make a difference, letting you run more models in memory and reducing loading and unloading. It also means that you can comfortably run other applications and AI models together, such as Visual Studio or DaVinci Resolve, with some impressive results. This use of running an AI Model alongside Visual Studio or DaVinci Resolve is where the real power comes into play, and from this angle the step up from the EVO-X3 to the EVO-X5 is greater. While this machine has AI potential, you can still use AI Managers and models to balance what you want the system to do. The final part of the test was to run a few games, and here again, the power of that CPU and integrated GPU was impressive, with Indiana Jones and the Great Circle running at 1080p extremely well. Likewise, Cyberpunk 2077. If you do want to increase the resolution and effects, then a dedicated eGPU would be a good idea, but out of the box, the performance is still impressive. At the end of this test, the machine more than proved its abilities and also enabled me to push testing and experimenting with local AI to a greater degree than I have been able to before. The main point for me that helps to balance the cost is the creative and admin potential. This machine rips through video, transcoding quickly when needed, and the auto video editing in DaVinci Resolve is incredibly impressive; however, as ever, there is a learning curve, as these features take time to set up. The EVO-X5 is an interesting machine and, without doubt, the most powerful AI-enhanced mini PC I have looked at so far. What surprises me is that the performance, while better in many respects than the EVO-X3, doesn’t feel much better to justify the current price difference. However, once you look at the current cost of RAM, that increase becomes apparent. If you are running the EVO-X3, it's a powerful AI machine and will do pretty much everything the EVO-X5 will do, though the process will be slightly different because it doesn’t have as much headroom in RAM capacity. I have also noted that newer local language models allocate resources better, so while many models thrive in this machine with that extra RAM, plenty of new-generation models are better adapted to memory allocation and seem to run as well on the EVO-X3 with its 128GB of RAM. However, in use, there’s no doubting this compact machine's speed and abilities. For standard office work, it’s exceptional, and for creative work, it’s surprisingly agile; with a dedicated eGPU to boost graphics processing, it will be a formidable option for video and photo editing. While this machine is decent for gaming, it’s not designed for it, so a quick dip into the gaming world after work is possible, and the gameplay quality is exceptional. However, if that is what you want the machine for, a dedicated gaming machine will be cheaper. The new CPU and enhanced RAM deliver the headline performance upgrades, and you can run larger models, making it what it is supposed to be; at present, most of that cost comes from the RAM. So if you want to run larger language models, you will need to stretch to this latest model. However, the EVO-X3 is still an excellent, cheaper option, and at present is equally impressive if slightly less powerful. Should I buy the GMKtec EVO-X5 Pro? Buy it if... You want to run large AI models locally. With its huge unified memory capacity and powerful processor, the EVO-X5 Pro can handle large language models locally that would push most conventional mini PCs beyond their limits. You need a powerful compact creative workstation. For large image libraries, 4K video editing, and AI-enhanced creative applications, the EVO-X5 Pro delivers excellent performance, fast networking, and extensive storage options in a compact design. Don't buy it if... You only need a mini PC for everyday work. For office applications, web browsing, and general creative work, the EVO-X5 Pro offers far more power than you need. Cheaper mini PCs, including the EVO-X3, provide better value. You need a workstation with powerful dedicated graphics. While the integrated graphics perform well, demanding 3D work and complex video editing benefit from a dedicated GPU. A conventional desktop workstation may offer better value. item.title: SALES: How a United credit card can save you hundreds of thousands of miles on flights
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
What if I told you that having a United credit card could mean the difference between paying 295,000 miles or just 72,000 miles for the exact same international business-class flight? That's not a rare or theoretical example. It's a real award flight that a friend of mine was trying to book recently. And while United's credit cards are currently offering welcome bonuses of up to 100,000 miles, there's another benefit that can be even more valuable long-term: Access to expanded saver award availability and dramatically lower award prices for eligible cardholders. In fact, on some flights, the savings can quite literally be hundreds of thousands of miles per ticket. Here's how it works — and why having a United credit card can make such a huge difference when it's time to redeem your miles. Apply here for a limited-time offer on the United Club℠ Card — Earn up to 100,000 bonus miles: Earn 90,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn an additional 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening (see rates and fees) Save hundreds of thousands of miles on flights A friend of mine was recently searching for business-class award flights from Geneva Airport (GVA) to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) for a trip next month. He knew United cardholders could access lower award prices, but he didn't have a United card, so he asked me to compare what we were seeing before deciding whether to apply. As a non-cardholder, he was seeing business-class prices of 295,000 United miles per person, plus taxes and fees for the one-way trip from Geneva to Newark. That's a lot of miles when multiplied out for a family. As a cardholder, I checked the same flights and saw a much lower price. For the same business-class flights, my price was just 68,000 miles per person, plus taxes and fees. That's 77% fewer miles for the same lie-flat seat on the same plane. Now, I have United elite status in addition to a United credit card, which brings my award price down a little further. But even without elite status, someone with an eligible United credit card could book that flight for just 72,000 miles. That's a savings of 223,000 miles on a single one-way ticket. Here's why the difference is so dramatic: The savings aren't simply the result of a 10% cardholder discount. Eligible United cardholders can also access expanded saver award availability, which can unlock significantly lower award prices on certain flights. And this isn't just one route or one date. I also searched for business-class award flights from my home airport of George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston to Sydney Airport (SYD) and quickly found a flight priced at 400,000 miles for someone without a United card. The cardmember-only price? Just 85,000 miles, plus taxes and fees. That's a savings of 315,000 miles — or nearly 79% — on a single award ticket. Multiply it out by a family, and it gets even more incredible in a hurry. Eligible United cardholders can save at least 10% on award flights While lots of United award flights have really big savings like the examples above, not every flight will offer discounts that dramatic. You'll always save at least 10% off qualifying United-operated award flights just by having a United card. That number jumps to at least 15% if you also have United elite status. So, to give another real-world example, my family flies several times a year between George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston and Orlando International Airport (MCO). On this example date, one-way flights were priced at either 15,000 or 21,000 United miles, depending on which flight I selected. However, because I have the United card, those flights were priced at 12,700 miles instead of 15,000 miles, or 17,800 miles instead of 21,000 miles. Those savings aren't as headline-grabbing as the first example, but for a family of four booking round-trip flights at those rates, the savings could add up to roughly 18,000 to 26,000 miles, depending on the flights selected. Even the no-annual-fee United cards can activate the savings One thing I really love about this is that you don't need a premium United card with a high annual fee to unlock these award savings. You can get the $0 annual fee United Gateway℠ Card (see rates and fees) and get savings, too. If you have the United MileagePlus® Debit Rewards card or the $0 annual fee United credit card, you do have to spend $10,000 in eligible purchases on those cards in a calendar year to unlock the award discount. For travelers who can meet that threshold through purchases they'd make anyway, the Gateway could provide a way to access lower award prices without paying an annual fee. Another option is the United℠ Explorer Card (see rates and fees), which actually has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 annually. Eligible Explorer cardholders can access the award discounts without meeting the Gateway's $10,000 spending requirement. United credit cards can offer more than bonus miles and travel perks. For eligible cardholders, access to expanded saver award availability and discounts on qualifying award flights can translate into substantial savings when redeeming MileagePlus miles. Being able to save airline miles with a co-branded airline credit card isn't unique to United, as several airlines offer this valuable perk to their cardholders. However, the mileage savings you get with most cards and airlines are often capped at around 15%. As the Geneva–Newark and Houston–Sydney examples show, the difference can sometimes amount to hundreds of thousands of miles on a single ticket. However, savings vary by flight, and not every cardholder automatically qualifies for these benefits. Being able to take a lie-flat seat across the globe and make it cost in the neighborhood of 70,000-85,000 miles instead of 300,000-400,000 miles, just by having a credit card is exactly the kind of tip that brings award travel out of just the hands of a small few and puts it into the hands of many of us.
